Chocolate brands.Hershey's: Hershey, Pennsylvania, was built around the chocolate factory by Milton Hershey and has streetlights shaped like Kisses.
Chocolate brands.Cadbury: Cadbury, founded in Birmingham in 1824, launched Dairy Milk in 1905, and it has been Britain's best-selling bar for decades.
Chocolate brands.Lindt: Lindt's Swiss chocolatier Rodolphe Lindt invented conching in 1879, a long mixing process that makes chocolate melt smoothly.
Chocolate brands.Godiva: Godiva, a Belgian premium chocolatier founded in 1926, took its name from Lady Godiva, the legend of the naked horse ride.
Chocolate brands.Ghirardelli: Ghirardelli, founded in San Francisco in 1852 during the Gold Rush, is among the oldest continuously operating chocolate makers in the US.
Chocolate brands.Milka: Milka's purple cow, Lila, is a famous mascot, and the brand began in Switzerland in 1901 with Alpine milk.
Chocolate brands.Ferrero Rocher: Ferrero Rocher, a hazelnut ball wrapped in gold foil, takes its name from a rock grotto at Lourdes, the French pilgrimage site.
Chocolate brands.Guylian: Guylian, a Belgian maker, is famed for its seashell pralines, which are shaped to honor the Belgian coast.
Chocolate brands.Valrhona: Valrhona, from France's Rhône valley, is a favorite of pastry chefs and a leader in single-origin chocolate.
Chocolate brands.Côte d'Or: Côte d'Or is a Belgian brand whose name is French for Gold Coast, and its elephant logo recalls the cocoa's origin in Africa.
Chocolate brands.Ritter Sport: Ritter Sport's square shape came from a 1930s idea for a bar that fits in a sports jacket pocket without breaking.
Chocolate brands.Green & Black's: Green & Black's launched Maya Gold in 1994, which became the first product in the UK to carry the Fairtrade mark.
Chocolate brands.Haribo: Haribo is a German gummy candy maker, best known for the gummy bear, and not a chocolate brand.
Chocolate brands.Jelly Belly: Jelly Belly makes gourmet jelly beans, not chocolate; Ronald Reagan kept a jar on his desk, and they flew on Air Force One.
Chocolate brands.Werther's: Werther's Original is a German buttery caramel candy, and it isn't a chocolate brand.
Chocolate brands.Mentos: Mentos are Dutch chewy mints, and when dropped into diet cola they make a geyser, a stunt that went viral online.
Chocolate brands.Chupa Chups: Chupa Chups lollipops come from Spain, and the daisy logo was designed by Salvador Dalí in 1969.
Chocolate brands.Trolli: Trolli is a German brand known for gummy candy, most famously the sour-coated gummy worms.
Chocolate brands.Ricola: Ricola is a Swiss herbal cough drop, with a famous yodeling ad, and has no chocolate in it.
Chocolate brands.Halls: Halls is a menthol cough drop that began in Britain in 1893 as a medicinal sweet.
Chocolate brands.Sour Patch Kids: Sour Patch Kids are sour-coated gummy candies that were first called Mars Men when they were created in Canada.
Chocolate brands.Nerds: Nerds are crunchy, tiny candy pieces from Wonka, with two flavors in each box, and they contain no chocolate.
Chocolate brands.Hubba Bubba: Hubba Bubba is a bubble gum launched in 1979 that was marketed as easy to blow big bubbles without sticking to the face.
Chocolate brands.Fisherman's Friend: Fisherman's Friend is a strong menthol lozenge, which was devised in Fleetwood, England, for trawlermen braving cold seas.

Plants poisonous to eat.Foxglove: Foxglove gives us the heart drug digoxin, but eaten raw it can trigger a dangerous irregular heartbeat.
Plants poisonous to eat.Oleander: Oleander is a popular shrub, yet every part of it contains cardiac toxins, and even its smoke or sap can be harmful.
Plants poisonous to eat.Hemlock: Poison hemlock is the plant Socrates is believed to have drunk, and it looks much like wild carrot, which makes mistakes deadly.
Plants poisonous to eat.Deadly nightshade: Deadly nightshade's glossy black berries look tempting, but a few can be fatal, and it is also called belladonna.
Plants poisonous to eat.Castor bean: Castor beans contain ricin, one of the most potent natural poisons, yet the same seeds yield castor oil.
Plants poisonous to eat.Lily of the valley: Lily of the valley has sweet-smelling bells and red berries, and all parts are toxic to the heart.
Plants poisonous to eat.Yew: Yew needles and seeds are highly toxic, but its bark yielded the cancer drug paclitaxel.
Plants poisonous to eat.Monkshood: Monkshood, also called wolfsbane, contains aconitine, one of the deadliest plant toxins, which can even absorb through skin.
Plants poisonous to eat.Rhubarb leaves: Rhubarb stalks make pies, but the leaves contain oxalic acid and are unsafe to eat.
Plants poisonous to eat.Daffodil bulbs: Daffodil bulbs look like onions, and eating them has caused real poisonings from the toxin lycorine.
Plants poisonous to eat.Basil: Basil is a safe, popular kitchen herb, and its sweet leaves are a classic partner of tomato.
Plants poisonous to eat.Mint: Mint is safe and spreads fast, so gardeners often grow it in pots to contain it.
Plants poisonous to eat.Lettuce: Lettuce is a safe salad staple, and wild lettuce's milky sap gave the plant its name in Latin, lactuca.
Plants poisonous to eat.Sunflower: Sunflower seeds are safe and nutritious, and the plant has long been grown for oil.
Plants poisonous to eat.Rose: Rose petals and hips are edible, and rose hips are rich in vitamin C, famously used for syrup in wartime Britain.
Plants poisonous to eat.Dandelion: Dandelion leaves, flowers and roots are all edible, and the root has been roasted as a coffee substitute.
Plants poisonous to eat.Chamomile: Chamomile is a gentle herb long used for tea, and it's a relative of the daisy.
Plants poisonous to eat.Spinach: Spinach is safe to eat, though rich in oxalates, and its fame as a strength food owes a lot to Popeye.
Plants poisonous to eat.Carrot: Carrots are safe to eat, and they were originally purple or white before orange types spread.
Plants poisonous to eat.Clover: Clover is edible, and its sweet flowers can be steeped for tea, and the leaves are eaten in salads.
Plants poisonous to eat.Thyme: Thyme is a safe aromatic herb and is rich in thymol, which is used in mouthwash.
Plants poisonous to eat.Rosemary: Rosemary is safe and fragrant, and it has long been a symbol of remembrance.
Plants poisonous to eat.Nasturtium: Nasturtium flowers and leaves are edible and peppery, with a flavor similar to watercress.
Plants poisonous to eat.Pumpkin: Pumpkin flesh, seeds and even blossoms are edible, and its seeds are a popular snack.

Animals where dads do the babysitting.Seahorse: A male seahorse carries the fertilised eggs in a brood pouch and gives birth, up to about a thousand babies. The female simply deposits the eggs.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Emperor penguin: The male emperor penguin balances a single egg on his feet through the Antarctic winter for about two months, without eating, while females go to sea.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Emu: Male emus incubate the eggs for about eight weeks, barely eating or drinking. Then they guard the chicks for months.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Rhea: The male rhea scrapes the nest, hosts several females' eggs, and raises the chicks alone. Rheas are the South American cousins of the ostrich.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Darwin's frog: In Darwin's frog, the male keeps tadpoles in his vocal sac. They develop there and hop out as tiny froglets.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Midwife toad: The male midwife toad wraps strings of eggs around his hind legs and carries them for weeks. He then dips into water for them to hatch.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Pipefish: Pipefish are relatives of seahorses, and the male carries the eggs, in a pouch or on his belly. They're slim and look like straightened seahorses.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Cassowary: The cassowary is a large flightless bird where the male does all the incubating and chick-rearing, for about nine months. It's also one of the most dangerous birds.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Jacana: Jacana males build nests and raise the chicks, often carrying them tucked under a wing. Their long toes let them walk on floating lily pads.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Stickleback: Male sticklebacks build a nest of plant material, guard the eggs, and fan them with their fins to keep them oxygenated.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Lion: Male lions mostly defend the territory, while lionesses do the hunting and raise the cubs. A new male taking over a pride may even kill the cubs.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Peacock: Peacocks display for females, then leave. The peahen alone incubates the eggs and raises the chicks.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Elephant: Male elephants live apart from the herd, and the care of calves is shared by females, called allomothers. Bulls take no part.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Mallard: Mallard drakes leave once the female starts incubating. The duck alone looks after the ducklings.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Grizzly bear: Male grizzlies play no part in raising cubs, and sometimes pose a danger to them. Mothers keep cubs for two to three years.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Orangutan: Orangutan fathers are mostly solitary. Mothers raise the young alone, nursing for up to about seven years, the slowest in any ape.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Leopard: Male leopards are solitary and take no part in rearing. The mother hides the cubs in dens and moves them often.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Deer: Stags take no part in raising fawns. Does hide the young, which have spots and almost no scent for protection.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Turkey: Male wild turkeys, called toms, mate with several hens and leave. The hen does all the nesting and chick-rearing.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Kangaroo: Male kangaroos don't raise the joey. The joey spends months in the mother's pouch, being only about the size of a jellybean at birth.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Cheetah: Male cheetahs live in small groups called coalitions, while the mother raises the cubs alone. She hides them in dense grass.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Koala: Female koalas carry joeys in the pouch for about six months, then on the back. The male has no role in caring for them.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.Hummingbird: Hummingbird males mate and leave. The female builds a tiny nest, often with spider silk, and raises the chicks alone.
Animals where dads do the babysitting.House cat: Tomcats play no part in raising kittens. Female cats can have multiple litters a year, which is why neutering matters.

Canadian foods.Poutine: Fries topped with cheese curds and gravy, from rural Quebec in the late 1950s; the curds should squeak.
Canadian foods.Butter tart: A small pastry with a gooey filling of butter, sugar and egg; the big debate is whether raisins belong in it.
Canadian foods.Nanaimo bar: A no-bake treat with a crumb base, custard and chocolate layers, named for Nanaimo in British Columbia.
Canadian foods.Tourtière: A spiced meat pie, traditionally eaten in Quebec at Christmas Eve, after midnight mass.
Canadian foods.Peameal bacon: Back bacon rolled in cornmeal, the filling of Toronto's famous sandwich at St. Lawrence Market; the name comes from old ground yellow peas.
Canadian foods.BeaverTails: Fried pastry shaped like a beaver's tail, topped with cinnamon sugar or chocolate, a popular treat on Ottawa's frozen canal.
Canadian foods.Ketchup chips: A snack flavour that is a Canadian favourite, with a sweet and sour tang, and hard to find in the USA.
Canadian foods.Montreal bagel: Smaller, sweeter and denser than a New York bagel, it is boiled in honey water and baked in a wood-fired oven.
Canadian foods.Bloody Caesar: A cocktail with vodka and clam-tomato juice, invented in Calgary in 1969, and often garnished with a celery stalk.
Canadian foods.Maple taffy: Boiling maple syrup is poured onto snow and rolled onto a stick, a Quebec sugar-shack tradition; Canada makes most of the world's maple syrup.
Canadian foods.Key lime pie: An American dessert from the Florida Keys, not Canadian.
Canadian foods.Cheesesteak: A Philadelphia sandwich, so not Canadian.
Canadian foods.Corn dog: An American fairground favourite, not Canadian.
Canadian foods.Gumbo: A Louisiana stew thickened with okra or roux, so a taste of the American South, not Canada.
Canadian foods.Grits: A Southern American porridge of ground corn, not Canadian.
Canadian foods.Pavlova: A meringue dessert from Australia and New Zealand, not Canadian.
Canadian foods.Lamington: An Australian cake covered in chocolate and coconut, not Canadian.
Canadian foods.Tim Tam: An Australian chocolate biscuit; the 'Tim Tam slam' means sipping a hot drink through it.
Canadian foods.Vegemite: An Australian yeast spread, and a trap since Canada has its own yeast spreads; it is not Canadian.
Canadian foods.Haggis: Scotland's famous dish of sheep offal and oats, traditionally honoured on Burns Night, and not Canadian.
Canadian foods.Pecan pie: An American Southern dessert, not Canadian.
Canadian foods.Fish and chips: A British dish, though the maritime provinces love it too, but not a Canadian original.
Canadian foods.Cornish pasty: A pastry from Cornwall, England, not Canadian.
Canadian foods.Jambalaya: A Louisiana rice dish with Creole and Spanish roots, so it is American rather than Canadian.

Flatbreads.Naan: An Indian leavened flatbread, traditionally slapped onto the walls of a hot clay tandoor oven, where it puffs up and blisters.
Flatbreads.Pita: Its steam puffs up the dough into a hollow pocket in a very hot oven, which makes it perfect for stuffing.
Flatbreads.Tortilla: Mexican tortillas are made of maize treated with lime (nixtamalised), which unlocks nutrients and goes back thousands of years.
Flatbreads.Lavash: A thin Armenian flatbread, baked on the walls of a tonir oven; UNESCO lists its making as an intangible cultural heritage.
Flatbreads.Roti: A simple, unleavened wholewheat flatbread cooked on a griddle, eaten daily across South Asia and the Caribbean.
Flatbreads.Chapati: An unleavened wheat flatbread eaten in India and East Africa, rolled thin and puffed on a hot pan.
Flatbreads.Paratha: A layered, buttery flatbread from South Asia, which is pan-fried and often stuffed with potato.
Flatbreads.Injera: Ethiopia's spongy, slightly sour flatbread, made from fermented teff flour, which doubles as the plate and the cutlery.
Flatbreads.Piadina: A thin flatbread from Romagna in Italy, which is cooked on a griddle and folded around ham and cheese.
Flatbreads.Matzo: The unleavened bread eaten at Passover, which must be baked in under 18 minutes so that it can't rise.
Flatbreads.Laffa: A large, soft Iraqi-Israeli flatbread baked in a tabun oven and used for wraps such as shawarma.
Flatbreads.Baguette: A long French loaf with a crisp crust that rises with yeast, so it isn't a flatbread.
Flatbreads.Brioche: A rich French bread enriched with butter and eggs, and it rises into a soft, fluffy loaf.
Flatbreads.Bagel: A ring of dough that is boiled before baking, giving it a chewy crust; it rises, so it isn't flat.
Flatbreads.Challah: A braided, egg-enriched Jewish bread for the Sabbath, so a leavened, tall loaf.
Flatbreads.Pumpernickel: A dense, dark German rye bread that is baked slowly for many hours; it is not flat.
Flatbreads.Croissant: A flaky, buttery crescent of laminated yeast dough, definitely not flat.
Flatbreads.Pretzel: A knotted bread dipped in lye before baking, so not flat.
Flatbreads.Soda bread: An Irish loaf raised with baking soda and buttermilk instead of yeast; it is quick, but a round loaf, not flat.
Flatbreads.Babka: A sweet, twisted yeast loaf swirled with chocolate or cinnamon, not a flatbread.
Flatbreads.Panettone: A tall, domed Italian Christmas bread, definitely not flat.
Flatbreads.Hot cross bun: A spiced sweet bun marked with a cross, traditionally eaten on Good Friday, and not flat.
Flatbreads.Sourdough: A loaf leavened with wild yeast and bacteria in a starter, so it rises and is not flat.
Flatbreads.Kaiser roll: A round bread roll with a pinwheel top, which is risen with yeast and not flat.

Legumes.Lentil: Lentils are among the oldest cultivated crops, grown in the Near East for roughly 9,000 years, and they cook without soaking.
Legumes.Chickpea: Chickpeas are the base of hummus and falafel, and the liquid from a can, called aquafaba, can be whipped into vegan meringue.
Legumes.Black bean: Black beans, a staple from Mexico to Brazil, get their dark color from anthocyanin pigments that also tint the cooking water purple.
Legumes.Kidney bean: Kidney beans contain a toxin, phytohaemagglutinin, so raw or undercooked ones can make you ill; boiling them properly destroys it.
Legumes.Pea: Gregor Mendel's famous genetics experiments were done on pea plants, which is why wrinkled versus round peas appear in every biology class.
Legumes.Peanut: Despite the name, the peanut ripens underground and is a legume, not a nut, which is why it sits closer to peas than to walnuts.
Legumes.Soybean: Soybeans supply tofu, soy milk, soy sauce and miso, and are one of the few plant foods with all the essential amino acids.
Legumes.Fava bean: Fava beans have been eaten since ancient times, but some people with a genetic enzyme deficiency can fall ill from them, a condition called favism.
Legumes.Lima bean: Lima beans are named after Lima, Peru, and some raw varieties contain cyanide-releasing compounds, so they must be cooked.
Legumes.Pinto bean: Pinto means painted in Spanish; the beans are speckled when raw, then lose the pattern and turn pinkish-brown when cooked.
Legumes.Mung bean: Mung beans are the sprout you find in stir-fries, and they are also ground into the paste inside many Asian desserts.
Legumes.Green bean: Green beans are simply immature bean pods picked before the seeds fatten, and the old-fashioned stringy kind needed the string pulled off.
Legumes.Tamarind: Tamarind is a legume too: its sticky, sour brown pulp comes from a pod, and it is a key flavor in Worcestershire sauce.
Legumes.Almond: Almonds are the seeds of a fruit related to peaches, and the almond tree is not a legume, so it belongs to the rose family instead.
Legumes.Cashew: Cashews grow dangling from a fleshy cashew apple, and the shell contains an irritant related to poison ivy, so they are never sold in the shell.
Legumes.Walnut: Walnuts are the seeds of a drupe, a fruit with a stone, and the wrinkled kernel's shape has long been compared to a brain.
Legumes.Coffee bean: Coffee beans are not beans at all but the seeds of a red cherry-like fruit, so they are not legumes despite the name.
Legumes.Cocoa bean: Cocoa beans are seeds from the pods of a tropical tree, not legumes, and were once used as currency by the Aztecs.
Legumes.Vanilla bean: Vanilla beans are fermented seed pods of an orchid, so they are not legumes; hand-pollination makes vanilla the second priciest spice by weight.
Legumes.Jelly bean: Quinoa is a seed from a plant related to spinach and beets, not a legume; Andean peoples have grown it for thousands of years.
Legumes.Quinoa: Jelly beans are candy named for their shape, with no plant bean inside, and each one traditionally takes days to make, including a shell-coating step.
Legumes.Corn: Corn is a grass, so it belongs with the cereals, not the legumes, though the old 'three sisters' farming planted it alongside beans.
Legumes.Sunflower seed: Sunflower seeds come from a composite flower head, a relative of daisies, so they are unrelated to legumes despite being pea-sized.
Legumes.Pistachio: Pistachios are seeds of a tree in the cashew family; the shell splits open on its own when ripe, which is why they are called the smiling nut.

US states on the Atlantic coast.Maine: Its coastline is so deeply indented that it stretches over 3,000 miles, longer than California's, and it is the easternmost state.
US states on the Atlantic coast.New Hampshire: It has only about 18 miles of coastline, the shortest of any Atlantic state, yet it holds the first-in-the-nation primary.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Massachusetts: Cape Cod, the state's hooked arm of sand, was shaped by glaciers, and Plymouth Rock marks the Pilgrim landing of 1620.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Rhode Island: The smallest state by area has roughly 400 miles of shoreline thanks to Narragansett Bay, and its full name is longer than any other state's.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Connecticut: Its short coast runs along Long Island Sound rather than directly onto the open Atlantic, but it still counts as an Atlantic coast state.
US states on the Atlantic coast.New York: Its Atlantic edge is mostly Long Island, which is home to the Hamptons and also holds Brooklyn and Queens.
US states on the Atlantic coast.New Jersey: With the Jersey Shore running over 100 miles, it is also where Atlantic City's boardwalk and Monopoly's street names come from.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Delaware: The first state to ratify the Constitution, in 1787, has Atlantic beaches at Rehoboth and Bethany.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Maryland: Ocean City sits on a barrier island facing the Atlantic, while the huge Chesapeake Bay cuts the rest of the state in two.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Virginia: It touches the Atlantic at Virginia Beach, and the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel crosses the mouth of the bay.
US states on the Atlantic coast.North Carolina: The Outer Banks, a chain of barrier islands, is where the Wright brothers first flew in 1903 at Kitty Hawk.
US states on the Atlantic coast.South Carolina: Charleston Harbor fronts the Atlantic, and the state's coast includes rich marshes and the Gullah Geechee culture.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Georgia: Its short coastline hides a string of Golden Isles, including Cumberland Island with its wild horses.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Florida: It has more coastline than any state in the lower 48, with the Atlantic on its east and the Gulf of Mexico on its west.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Vermont: Trap: this New England state is landlocked, bordered by Lake Champlain rather than any ocean.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Pennsylvania: Trap: it feels like an East Coast state, but it has no ocean shore, only a bit of Lake Erie and the Delaware River estuary.
US states on the Atlantic coast.West Virginia: Trap: this Appalachian state is landlocked and often confused with Virginia, which does reach the coast.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Ohio: Trap: it reaches the Great Lakes at Lake Erie, which is a long way from the Atlantic.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Tennessee: Trap: it borders eight states but no ocean, famous for Nashville's music and the Great Smoky Mountains.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Alabama: Trap: it touches the Gulf of Mexico, not the Atlantic, at Mobile Bay.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Kentucky: Trap: this landlocked state is known for bourbon, horse racing, and Mammoth Cave, the longest known cave system in the world.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Louisiana: Trap: it borders the Gulf of Mexico, so its coast is Gulf rather than Atlantic.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Michigan: Trap: it has more Great Lakes shoreline than any other state but no ocean access.
US states on the Atlantic coast.Texas: Trap: its long Gulf coast, over 350 miles, is on the Gulf of Mexico, not the Atlantic.

Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Santa Claus: This Indiana town gets hundreds of thousands of letters to Santa each year, which volunteers answer.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Chicken: A tiny Alaska gold-mining town named after the ptarmigan, since the founders could not agree on how to spell it.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Hot Coffee: A Mississippi community named for a roadside stand that sold coffee made with moonshine.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Peculiar: This Missouri town incorporated in 1868 after the name it asked for had been taken, and its motto is 'Where the odds are with you'.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Toad Suck: An Arkansas community whose name is said to come from boatmen who sucked on whiskey bottles while waiting on the river.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Monkey's Eyebrow: This Kentucky community is said to be shaped like a monkey's eyebrow on the map.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Ding Dong: A tiny Texas community whose name comes from a general store founded by two partners whose bell-like nicknames stuck.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Accident: A Maryland town whose name is said to stem from two surveyors who unknowingly claimed the same tract, by accident.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Embarrass: A Minnesota town that is among the coldest places in the lower 48, with its name from a French word for obstacle.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Why: An Arizona town named for the Y-shaped junction of two highways, which is why its name is spelled Why.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Great Snoring: Trap: an English village in Norfolk, so it is British rather than American.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Westward Ho!: Trap: a village in Devon, and the only place in the UK with an exclamation mark in its name.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Mousehole: Trap: a Cornish fishing village, pronounced 'Mowzel', in England.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Wetwang: Trap: a Yorkshire village in England, and its name comes from an old term for a field for trial.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Barton in the Beans: Trap: a Leicestershire village in England, named for the beans grown there.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Pity Me: Trap: a County Durham village in England, whose name may come from the French petit mer, a small lake.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Ugley: Trap: an Essex village in England, whose name probably comes from an Old English personal name, not looks.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Dull: Trap: a village in Scotland, which has twinned with Boring, Oregon, and Bland, Australia.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Giggleswick: Trap: a North Yorkshire village in England, and a well-known school stands there.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Nether Wallop: Trap: a Hampshire village in England, whose neighbor is Over Wallop.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Matching Tye: Trap: an Essex village in England, near Matching Green.
Funny town names in the USA (not the UK).Lower Slaughter: Trap: a Cotswold village in England, whose name comes from an old word for a muddy place.

Places in Alaska.Anchorage: Alaska's largest city holds roughly 40 percent of the state's residents, and moose regularly wander through its neighborhoods.
Places in Alaska.Juneau: The capital city can be reached only by air or sea; no roads connect it to the rest of Alaska or Canada.
Places in Alaska.Fairbanks: Interior hub where winter temperatures can drop below minus 40, with some of the best aurora viewing around.
Places in Alaska.Denali: North America's tallest peak, at about 6,190 meters, officially renamed from Mount McKinley in 2015, its Koyukon name means the high one.
Places in Alaska.Kodiak: Home of the Kodiak brown bear, among the largest bears in the world, living on an island of the same name.
Places in Alaska.Ketchikan: Known as the salmon capital of the world, built on stilts and boardwalks on a rainy island shore.
Places in Alaska.Sitka: Once the capital of Russian America, with St. Michael's Cathedral still standing, and sold to the US in 1867.
Places in Alaska.Nome: The finish of the Iditarod sled dog race and the site of a famous 1900 gold rush.
Places in Alaska.Glacier Bay: A park where glaciers have retreated enormously since 1750, leaving a fjord system for whales to visit.
Places in Alaska.Kenai: A peninsula of fjords, fishing and glaciers, noted for the Kenai River's giant king salmon.
Places in Alaska.Prudhoe Bay: Site of North America's largest oil field, the start of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline.
Places in Alaska.Whitehorse: Canada's Yukon capital sits just over the border and is not in Alaska.
Places in Alaska.Yellowknife: Canada's Northwest Territories capital, sitting on Great Slave Lake, with a gold-mining history.
Places in Alaska.Vancouver: A major Canadian port in British Columbia, not in Alaska, which lies to the north.
Places in Alaska.Seattle: The largest city in Washington state, the closest big US city to Alaska, but still outside it.
Places in Alaska.Banff: Canada's oldest national park, founded in 1885 around hot springs in the Rockies of Alberta, well south of Alaska.
Places in Alaska.Churchill: A Manitoba town in Canada known as the polar bear capital of the world.
Places in Alaska.Iqaluit: The capital of Nunavut in Canada, an Arctic city whose name means place of many fish.
Places in Alaska.Siberia: A Russian region only about 90 kilometers across the Bering Strait from Alaska, so close but not in Alaska.
Places in Alaska.Nuuk: The Greenland capital is in another Arctic region, a self-governing part of Denmark.
Places in Alaska.Kamchatka: A Russian volcanic peninsula across the Bering Sea from Alaska, with many active volcanoes.
Places in Alaska.Svalbard: A Norwegian Arctic archipelago, on the other side of the Arctic from Alaska.
Places in Alaska.Dawson City: A Yukon town that boomed in the 1898 Klondike Gold Rush, in Canada, near the Alaska border.
Places in Alaska.Jasper: An Alberta national park in the Canadian Rockies, a dark sky preserve far from Alaska.

Parts of the brain.Cerebrum: The biggest part of the brain, divided into two hemispheres. Its wrinkled outer layer handles thought, language and voluntary movement.
Parts of the brain.Cerebellum: Latin for little brain, tucked at the back, holds over half the brain's neurons. It coordinates balance and smooth movement.
Parts of the brain.Brainstem: It connects the brain to the spinal cord and automatically runs breathing, heartbeat and sleep. Damage here is often life-threatening.
Parts of the brain.Hippocampus: Named for the Greek for seahorse, which it resembles. It's crucial for forming new memories, and it is one of the first areas hit by Alzheimer's.
Parts of the brain.Hypothalamus: Roughly the size of an almond, it regulates temperature, hunger, thirst and sleep, and controls the pituitary gland.
Parts of the brain.Thalamus: A relay station sending nearly all sensory signals, except smell, up to the cortex.
Parts of the brain.Amygdala: An almond-shaped cluster that processes emotion, particularly fear. Its name is Greek for almond.
Parts of the brain.Frontal lobe: The region behind the forehead that handles planning, decisions and personality. It matures last, usually into the mid-20s.
Parts of the brain.Medulla oblongata: The lowest part of the brainstem. It controls breathing and heart rate, and triggers reflexes like vomiting and coughing.
Parts of the brain.Corpus callosum: A thick bundle of about 200 million fibers connecting the left and right hemispheres so they can share information.
Parts of the brain.Pons: Latin for bridge, this part of the brainstem relays signals between the cerebrum and cerebellum and helps regulate sleep and breathing.
Parts of the brain.Cochlea: A trap: it belongs to the inner ear, a coiled tube that turns sound vibrations into nerve signals.
Parts of the brain.Retina: A trap: it's at the back of the eye. It is actually an outgrowth of the brain in embryo development.
Parts of the brain.Larynx: A trap: the voice box sits in the throat, not the brain, and holds the vocal cords that let you speak.
Parts of the brain.Thyroid: A trap: this butterfly-shaped gland sits in the neck, not the brain, and its hormones control the body's metabolism.
Parts of the brain.Aorta: A trap: the body's largest artery leaves the heart, and carries blood toward the brain but is not part of it.
Parts of the brain.Alveoli: A trap: these are the tiny air sacs of the lungs, not the brain. A person has hundreds of millions of them.
Parts of the brain.Pancreas: A trap: this gland sits behind the stomach in the abdomen, not in the head, and makes insulin to control blood sugar.
Parts of the brain.Spleen: A trap: it's an organ in the upper left abdomen that filters blood, not a part of the brain.
Parts of the brain.Tibia: A trap: the shinbone is in your lower leg, nowhere near the brain, and is the second-longest bone in the body.
Parts of the brain.Atrium: A trap: it's an upper chamber of the heart, not part of the brain. The word means entrance hall in Latin.
Parts of the brain.Diaphragm: A trap: the dome of muscle under the lungs that powers breathing, far from the brain, though the brain tells it when to contract.
Parts of the brain.Esophagus: A trap: the food tube from throat to stomach, about 25 centimeters long, belongs to digestion rather than the brain.
Parts of the brain.Femur: A trap: the thigh bone is far from the brain, and is the longest bone in the human body.

Bioluminescent (make their own light).Firefly: Fireflies are beetles whose 'cold light' wastes almost no heat. Each species flashes its own pattern to find a mate.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Anglerfish: Deep-sea females dangle a glowing lure on a rod from the head. Glowing bacteria living in the lure make the light.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Glowworm: In New Zealand caves, glowworm larvae hang glowing silk threads to lure insects. The light is made by the larvae, not adults.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Lanternfish: One of the most abundant fish in the ocean, with light organs along the body. Each night they rise to feed near the surface.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Firefly squid: A small Japanese squid whose blue lights shimmer in Toyama Bay each spring. It has light organs on its arms and body.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Dinoflagellates: Tiny plankton that make waves glow blue when disturbed. Some blooms light up bays at night.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Vampire squid: Despite its scary name, it eats marine snow, floating debris. It can turn itself inside out, and glow from tips of its arms.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Ghost mushroom: A pale, eerie Australian mushroom (Omphalotus nidiformis) that gives off a faint green glow, which is rare among fungi.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Crystal jelly: A jellyfish from the Pacific Northwest. Its glowing protein, GFP, was extracted by Osamu Shimomura and became a major tool in biology.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Hatchetfish: A deep-sea fish with light organs on the belly to hide its silhouette. By matching the faint light from above, it vanishes from predators below.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Clownfish: Famous from Finding Nemo. Its orange color is pigment, and it doesn't make its own light.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Goldfish: Its color is pigment that reflects light, not glowing. Goldfish can see infrared and ultraviolet light, though.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Moth: Moths don't glow. Some species are drawn to lights, though why they do so is still debated.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Peacock: Its shimmering feathers get their color from microscopic structures that reflect light. There's no light of its own.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Butterfly: Many butterflies shimmer, as the iridescent Morpho does, but that is structure reflecting light, not bioluminescence.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Electric eel: A trap: it makes electricity, up to about 600 volts, but not light. It's actually a knifefish, not a true eel.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Chameleon: Chameleons change color through tiny crystals in skin cells. They are reflecting light, not making any.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Bumblebee: Bees don't glow, though some flowers show patterns bees can see under ultraviolet light.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Flamingo: The pink comes from carotenoid pigments in the shrimp and algae they eat, not from any light production.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Poison dart frog: Its bright colors are a warning to predators, not a lamp. Its toxins come from the ants and other insects it eats.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Stingray: Stingrays make no light. They bury themselves in sand for camouflage, and the venomous spine on their tail is for defense.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Cuttlefish: Cuttlefish flash color waves on their skin, which is pigment and reflectors, not light production.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Mandrill: Its blue and red face colors shine in daylight but not in the dark. They are produced by skin structures, not bioluminescence.
Bioluminescent (make their own light).Parrot: Parrot feathers glow under UV light, but it's fluorescence, which needs outside light, and not true bioluminescence.

Movie musicals (the characters sing).Grease: The 1978 film paired John Travolta with Olivia Newton-John, and Barry Gibb of the Bee Gees wrote its title song.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).The Sound of Music: Based on the real Von Trapp family, the 1965 film won five Oscars including Best Picture.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).West Side Story: A Romeo and Juliet retelling in 1950s New York; the 1961 film won ten Oscars, a record for a musical.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Mamma Mia!: A story built entirely from ABBA songs, filmed on the Greek island of Skopelos.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Chicago: The 2002 film won Best Picture, the first musical to do so since Oliver! in 1968.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Les Miserables: In the 2012 film, the actors sang live on set instead of lip-syncing to a recording.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Cats: The 2019 film adapts Andrew Lloyd Webber's musical, based on T. S. Eliot's poems about cats.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).The Greatest Showman: Hugh Jackman plays P. T. Barnum; its soundtrack became one of the best-selling albums of 2018.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).La La Land: At the 2017 Oscars it was mistakenly announced as Best Picture before the real winner, Moonlight, was named.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Mary Poppins: Julie Andrews won Best Actress for this 1964 film, her first.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Wicked: The 2024 film tells the Wizard of Oz story from the Wicked Witch's side.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Annie: Based on the Little Orphan Annie comic strip, and it features the song Tomorrow.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Hairspray: A musical based on John Waters's 1988 film about 1960s Baltimore dancers.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Into the Woods: Sondheim's mash-up of fairy tales. Meryl Streep earned an Oscar nomination as the Witch in the 2014 film.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Titanic: Celine Dion's My Heart Will Go On plays over the credits, but no character sings it, and the film won eleven Oscars.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Rocky: Gonna Fly Now plays over the training montage, but it's a score, not characters singing.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Top Gun: Maverick and Goose sing You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin' in a bar, a rare moment, but not a musical.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Jaws: The only singing is Quint, Brody and Hooper's drunken sea shanty on the boat.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Speed: A 1994 thriller; the bus jump over a gap was filmed on an unfinished freeway.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Ghost: Its pottery scene boosted Unchained Melody, but the characters aren't singing.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Gladiator: Hans Zimmer and Lisa Gerrard's score matters more than any singing.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Casablanca: As Time Goes By and a patriotic Marseillaise singalong appear, but it's a drama.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).The Godfather: Nino Rota's score is famous, but this crime epic has no musical numbers.
Movie musicals (the characters sing).Die Hard: A Christmas Eve action film with Beethoven's Ode to Joy playing, but it's not a musical.

Nursery rhymes.Twinkle Twinkle: The words are from a 1806 poem by Jane Taylor, set to a French tune that Mozart also used for variations.
Nursery rhymes.Humpty Dumpty: Nowhere in the rhyme does it say Humpty is an egg; that picture came from Lewis Carroll and illustrators.
Nursery rhymes.Baa Baa Black Sheep: The rhyme goes back to at least 1744, and the 'one for the master' lines may reflect medieval wool taxes.
Nursery rhymes.Hickory Dickory Dock: The rhyme's clock may be one at Exeter Cathedral, which has a small hole in the door for a cat.
Nursery rhymes.Jack and Jill: The tale of Jack and Jill, who fell down the hill, has been told since the 1700s, and some claim it relates to royal taxes.
Nursery rhymes.Little Bo Peep: Bo Peep is a shepherdess who loses her sheep in a rhyme from the early 1800s, and the sheep come home on their own.
Nursery rhymes.Hey Diddle Diddle: The cat, fiddle, cow and moon rhyme was in print by 1765, and the dish running away with the spoon is its best-known line.
Nursery rhymes.Old King Cole: The merry old soul may be based on a legendary British king, and the rhyme was in print in the early 1700s.
Nursery rhymes.Ring a Ring o' Roses: A popular belief ties it to the Great Plague, but historians say that link is a later myth.
Nursery rhymes.Three Blind Mice: Its tune appeared in print in 1609, making it one of the oldest English nursery rhymes in print.
Nursery rhymes.Pop Goes the Weasel: In old London slang, a 'weasel' may be a tool or coat, and 'pop' meant pawn, so the weasel went off to the pawnshop.
Nursery rhymes.Georgie Porgie: This rhyme about a boy who kissed girls and ran off is from the 1800s and may be about a politician.
Nursery rhymes.Jingle Bells: Trap: a Christmas song from the 1850s, not a nursery rhyme, even though children sing it.
Nursery rhymes.Happy Birthday: Trap: it is a modern song with a known composer, which sets it apart from anonymous traditional rhymes.
Nursery rhymes.Silent Night: Trap: this is a Christmas carol first sung in 1818 in Austria, not a nursery rhyme.
Nursery rhymes.Yellow Submarine: Trap: a 1966 Beatles children's song, but a pop single, not a traditional rhyme.
Nursery rhymes.Let It Go: Trap: from Disney's Frozen in 2013, so it is a film song rather than a traditional rhyme.
Nursery rhymes.Hakuna Matata: Trap: it is from Disney's The Lion King; the phrase means 'no worries' in Swahili.
Nursery rhymes.Over the Rainbow: Trap: Judy Garland's 1939 song from The Wizard of Oz is a film standard, not a nursery rhyme.
Nursery rhymes.Auld Lang Syne: Trap: a Scots song, collected by Robert Burns, that is sung at New Year, not a rhyme for toddlers.
Nursery rhymes.Amazing Grace: Trap: John Newton wrote this hymn in the 1770s, and it is not a nursery rhyme.
Nursery rhymes.Greensleeves: Trap: a 16th-century English tune, long associated with Christmas as 'What Child Is This?', not a nursery rhyme.
Nursery rhymes.Danny Boy: Trap: its words were written in 1910 by Fred Weatherly, and it is far from a nursery song.
Nursery rhymes.Waltzing Matilda: Trap: Australia's best-known folk song is a ballad about a swagman, not a nursery rhyme.

Cards in a classic Uno deck.Skip: Skip makes the next player lose their turn. In the early 1970s, it was one of the first action cards that defined Uno.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Reverse: Reverse flips the direction of play, and in a two-player game it acts exactly like a Skip.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Draw Two: Draw Two forces the next player to draw two cards and lose their turn, and it comes in each of the four colours.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Wild: Wild lets the player choose the next colour, and each deck has four of them.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Wild Draw Four: Wild Draw Four lets you choose the colour and make the next player draw four, but you can only play it when you have no matching colour, or you can be challenged.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Red: Red is one of the four colours in Uno, along with blue, green and yellow.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Blue: Blue is one of the four colours, and every colour has 25 cards.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Green: Green is one of the four colours in the classic deck.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Yellow: Yellow is one of the four colours, and a standard deck has 108 cards.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Joker: Joker cards appear in a standard 52-card deck set as wildcards, but Uno's deck of 108 cards has Wild cards instead of Jokers.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Ace: An ace is a standard card and doesn't exist in Uno, whose numbered cards run 0 to 9 in four colours.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.King: Kings and other face cards belong to standard decks, while Uno cards carry only numbers, symbols and colours.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Purple: Uno has just four colours: red, yellow, green and blue. Purple was added only in some special editions and spin-offs.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Orange: The classic deck has no orange cards, and Uno's four colours were chosen for simplicity, so anyone can tell them apart.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Pink: Pink is not one of Uno's four colours, though special editions have used different shades and themes over the years.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Draw Three: Draw Three isn't in classic Uno, which has only Draw Two and Wild Draw Four. Some spin-offs add other draw cards.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Freeze: Freeze is not part of the classic deck; the Skip card is its nearest match, as it makes the next player lose a turn.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Bomb: Bomb doesn't exist in classic Uno, although variant decks and house rules invent plenty of extra explosive cards.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Trump: Trump is a feature of bridge and whist, where one suit outranks others, while Uno has no trump and its colours are equal.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Jack: Jack belongs to standard card decks, not Uno, where the only special cards are Skip, Reverse, Draw Two and the Wilds.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Queen: Queen is a face card in a standard deck, and Uno has no royalty, whose action cards are symbols such as Reverse and Skip.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Pass: Pass is not a card in Uno. If you cannot play, you draw from the pile, so the Skip card is the closest thing.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Brown: Steal isn't in classic Uno, though house rules like swapping hands appear in some variants, and the official Wild Swap Hands card does that.
Cards in a classic Uno deck.Steal: Brown is not an Uno colour, and the classic deck's four are bright primaries to remain distinct at a glance.

Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Acropolis: The high city of Athens, which holds the Parthenon and the Erechtheion.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Delphi: The Greeks viewed the oracle of Apollo as the center of the world, marked by a stone called the omphalos.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Olympia: The ancient Olympic Games began here in 776 BC, and the modern torch is still lit here.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Knossos: The Minoan palace on Crete is linked to the Minotaur legend. Arthur Evans partly reconstructed it in the early 1900s.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Mycenae: Agamemnon's legendary city has the Lion Gate, and Schliemann found a golden mask in 1876.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Epidaurus: Its theater has such fine acoustics that a whisper on stage can be heard in the top rows, and plays are still staged.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Delos: A sacred island, the legendary birthplace of Apollo, where births and burials were banned.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Cape Sounion: Its Temple of Poseidon stands on a cliff, and Lord Byron carved his name into a column.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Vergina: Its tombs held royal Macedonian burials, probably including Philip II, Alexander the Great's father.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Ancient Corinth: A rich trading city on an isthmus whose name gave us the Corinthian column.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Parthenon: The temple of Athena was largely destroyed in 1687, when a Venetian shell hit Ottoman gunpowder stored inside.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Pompeii: The Roman city near Naples was buried by Vesuvius in AD 79. It is in Italy.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Colosseum: Rome's great amphitheater is in Italy, not Greece, and opened in AD 80.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Ephesus: A Greek city, but its ruins, including the Temple of Artemis, a wonder of the world, are in Turkey.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Troy: The legendary city of the Trojan War lies in northwest Turkey, on the Dardanelles.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Petra: The rock-cut city of the Nabataeans is in Jordan, and was made famous by the Indiana Jones films.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Carthage: Rome's great rival stood on the coast of Tunisia, in North Africa, and was destroyed in 146 BC.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Luxor: This Egyptian city holds the temples of Karnak and the Valley of the Kings, not Greece.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Giza: The Great Pyramid and the Sphinx stand in Egypt, outside Cairo, and not in Greece.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Persepolis: The ceremonial capital of Persia is in southern Iran, burned by Alexander in 330 BC.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Babylon: The ancient Mesopotamian capital lies in Iraq, south of Baghdad, not in Greece.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Leptis Magna: A spectacular Roman city on the coast of Libya, birthplace of the emperor Septimius Severus.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Herculaneum: Pompeii's neighbor, buried by Vesuvius in AD 79, lies in Italy, not Greece.
Ancient sites in modern-day Greece.Pergamon: The Greek city famed for its library and altar is in Turkey; the altar is in a Berlin museum.

Famous pioneering aviators.Amelia Earhart: The American who vanished in 1937 near Howland Island during her round-the-world attempt. In 1932 she became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic.
Famous pioneering aviators.Wright brothers: Orville and Wilbur made the first powered, controlled flight in 1903 at Kitty Hawk. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet.
Famous pioneering aviators.Charles Lindbergh: In 1927 he made the first solo non-stop flight across the Atlantic, in the Spirit of St. Louis, from New York to Paris in about 33 hours.
Famous pioneering aviators.Red Baron: German World War I ace Manfred von Richthofen, named for his red plane. He shot down 80 aircraft before his death in 1918.
Famous pioneering aviators.Bessie Coleman: In 1921 she became the first African American woman to hold a pilot's licence, earned in France because American schools refused her.
Famous pioneering aviators.Louis Bleriot: In 1909 he made the first flight across the English Channel, in a monoplane, in roughly 37 minutes.
Famous pioneering aviators.Amy Johnson: A British pilot who in 1930 flew solo from England to Australia, becoming a national heroine. She died in 1941 while serving in the Air Transport Auxiliary.
Famous pioneering aviators.Chuck Yeager: The first pilot confirmed to break the sound barrier, in 1947 in the Bell X-1. He did it two days after breaking ribs in a horse accident.
Famous pioneering aviators.Howard Hughes: A billionaire who set a round-the-world speed record in 1938. He also built the 'Spruce Goose', the largest wooden aircraft ever flown.
Famous pioneering aviators.Saint-Exupery: The author of The Little Prince, who was a pilot. He vanished on a reconnaissance flight in 1944, and wreckage was found decades later.
Famous pioneering aviators.Douglas Bader: A British pilot who lost both legs in a 1931 crash but returned to fly Spitfires in World War II. He was shot down and captured in 1941.
Famous pioneering aviators.Jean Batten: A New Zealand pilot who in 1936 flew solo from England to New Zealand, a record. She was well known in her country.
Famous pioneering aviators.Henry Ford: Trap: an automaker whose assembly line made cars cheap, but he was a car maker, not a pilot, and he built the Model T.
Famous pioneering aviators.Thomas Edison: Trap: Edison developed the phonograph and a practical light bulb, a great inventor, but he was not an aviator.
Famous pioneering aviators.Karl Benz: Trap: the German engineer who built the first practical petrol-powered car in 1885, an automobile pioneer rather than aviator.
Famous pioneering aviators.Robert Fulton: Trap: American engineer who built a successful commercial steamboat in 1807. A pioneer of the water, not the air.
Famous pioneering aviators.Jacques Cousteau: Trap: the French ocean explorer who co-invented the aqualung, a pioneer of diving, not flying.
Famous pioneering aviators.Edmund Hillary: Trap: the New Zealand mountaineer who, with Tenzing Norgay, first reached Everest's summit in 1953. Not an aviator.
Famous pioneering aviators.Ernest Shackleton: Trap: the Anglo-Irish explorer of Antarctica. His Endurance expedition survived after a ship was crushed by ice, but he flew no planes.
Famous pioneering aviators.Robert Peary: Trap: the American explorer who claimed to reach the North Pole in 1909, a claim still debated, not a pilot.
Famous pioneering aviators.Marco Polo: Trap: a Venetian merchant whose travels to China in the 1200s were famed. An explorer, but of the Silk Road, not the air.
Famous pioneering aviators.Henry Morton Stanley: Trap: the journalist-explorer who found Livingstone in Africa in 1871. Overland explorer, not aviator.
Famous pioneering aviators.Isambard Brunel: Trap: Isambard Brunel built bridges, tunnels and ships such as the SS Great Eastern. An engineer, not an aviator.
Famous pioneering aviators.George Stephenson: Trap: the English railway pioneer behind the Rocket locomotive, an engineer of the rails, not the skies.

Types of tape.Duct tape: Duct tape was developed in World War II to seal ammunition cases, and soldiers called it duck tape because water ran off like it does off a duck.
Types of tape.Masking tape: Masking tape was invented in 1925 by Richard Drew of 3M, who was watching painters struggle with sticky tape that ruined paint jobs.
Types of tape.Scotch tape: Scotch tape got its name when a frustrated painter told 3M's sales team to take it back to its stingy Scotch bosses.
Types of tape.Electrical tape: Electrical tape is made of stretchy PVC vinyl, which insulates wires and stays flexible in the cold.
Types of tape.Packing tape: Packing tape is made of polypropylene, and it is made to stick to cardboard boxes to seal them.
Types of tape.Double-sided tape: Double-sided tape has glue on both faces, and it can mount posters or hold down carpets without nails.
Types of tape.Painter's tape: Painter's tape is a low-tack tape that comes off cleanly, so you get sharp paint lines without peeling the wall.
Types of tape.Washi tape: Washi tape is made of Japanese paper, and crafters love it because it peels away cleanly and tears by hand.
Types of tape.Gaffer tape: Gaffer tape is used by film and stage crews because it holds well but leaves no sticky residue, unlike duct tape.
Types of tape.Medical tape: Medical tape holds dressings to skin, and the breathable paper kind is made to peel off without tearing skin.
Types of tape.Glue stick: A glue stick is a solid paste, not a tape; the first one was launched by Henkel in 1969.
Types of tape.Staples: Staples are metal fasteners, and they pierce paper instead of sticking to it.
Types of tape.Velcro: Velcro was invented by Swiss engineer George de Mestral, who copied the burrs that stuck to his dog's fur.
Types of tape.Paper clip: A paper clip holds papers together with spring tension and no adhesive, and its familiar loop shape dates back to the 1890s.
Types of tape.Superglue: Superglue was discovered by accident in 1942 when chemists found a compound that stuck to everything.
Types of tape.Rubber cement: Rubber cement is a liquid glue, and it peels off without leaving a residue, so it is not a tape.
Types of tape.Blu Tack: Blu Tack is a reusable putty adhesive and was invented in the UK, and is shaped by hand rather than rolled out.
Types of tape.Thumbtack: A thumbtack pins things up with a point, rather than sticking them with adhesive.
Types of tape.Sticky note: The sticky note came about when a 3M scientist's weak glue found use as bookmarks in a hymnal.
Types of tape.Zip tie: A zip tie is a plastic strap with a locking head, and it was originally invented to bundle aircraft wires.
Types of tape.Binder clip: The binder clip was invented in 1910 by Louis Baltzley, and its two wire arms swing down to make handles.
Types of tape.Rubber band: The rubber band was patented in 1845 in England, and the first ones were made from natural rubber.
Types of tape.Twine: Twine is a string made of twisted fibers, so it holds by tying and not by sticking.
Types of tape.Glue dots: Glue dots are sticky dots and not a roll of tape.

Things that tell you the time.Wall clock: Hung on the wall since the 1300s in mechanical form, wall clocks began as huge church-tower clocks shrunk down for homes.
Things that tell you the time.Wristwatch: Early wristwatches were considered women's jewelry; soldiers in the First World War made them mainstream for hands-free timekeeping.
Things that tell you the time.Sundial: Sundials only work in daylight, and the shadow's hour lines must be tuned to the latitude where the dial sits.
Things that tell you the time.Smartphone: Phones get the exact time from network or GPS signals, making them far more accurate than most clocks people own.
Things that tell you the time.Microwave display: The little clock on a microwave is the one most people see daily, yet it usually blinks 12:00 after every power cut.
Things that tell you the time.Cuckoo clock: The cuckoo clock comes from Germany's Black Forest, and the bird's call is made by two small bellows and whistle pipes.
Things that tell you the time.Alarm clock: The first alarm clocks could ring only at one fixed hour; adjustable ones arrived in the 1800s.
Things that tell you the time.Big Ben: Big Ben is actually the bell, not the tower; the clock tower in London was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012.
Things that tell you the time.Smartwatch: Smartwatches can sync to atomic-clock time, but their first job for many owners is tracking steps and heart rate.
Things that tell you the time.Grandfather clock: A grandfather clock gets its name from an 1876 song, 'My Grandfather's Clock', about a clock that stopped when its owner died.
Things that tell you the time.Laptop: A laptop's clock is set by network time servers, which themselves trace back to atomic clocks around the world.
Things that tell you the time.Oven clock: Oven clocks are famous for being wrong; many people never reset them after a power cut and just do the math.
Things that tell you the time.Hourglass: An hourglass measures a fixed span, not the time of day, so it can't tell you whether it's morning or evening.
Things that tell you the time.Egg timer: Egg timers count down a set period, but they say nothing of the actual clock time.
Things that tell you the time.Stopwatch: A stopwatch measures elapsed time from when you press start, not the time of day, so it fails here.
Things that tell you the time.Metronome: A metronome clicks out beats per minute, so it divides time for musicians rather than telling the hour.
Things that tell you the time.Calendar: A calendar tells you the date, not the hour, so it tracks days while a clock tracks the time inside them.
Things that tell you the time.Thermometer: A thermometer measures temperature; Fahrenheit's mercury version in 1714 was the first truly reliable one.
Things that tell you the time.Compass: A compass points to magnetic north, giving direction but no hint about the hour.
Things that tell you the time.Barometer: A barometer tracks air pressure to forecast weather; falling pressure usually warns of storms.
Things that tell you the time.Kitchen scale: A kitchen scale weighs ingredients and has no idea what time it is, however precise its grams.
Things that tell you the time.Speedometer: A speedometer shows how fast you go, and speed is distance over time, but it can't tell you the time itself.
Things that tell you the time.Ruler: A ruler measures length; by itself it can't tell time, though rulers helped build sundial lines.
Things that tell you the time.Weather vane: A weather vane shows wind direction; the cockerel on top is a tradition tied to a ninth-century papal decree.

Things surgeons can transplant.Heart: Christiaan Barnard performed the first human heart transplant in Cape Town in 1967, and the patient lived 18 days.
Things surgeons can transplant.Kidney: Kidneys are the most transplanted organ, and living donors can give one and stay healthy with the other.
Things surgeons can transplant.Liver: A liver transplant can use part of a living donor's liver, since both the donor's and recipient's pieces regrow.
Things surgeons can transplant.Lung: The first lasting human lung transplants came in the early 1980s, long after kidneys and hearts.
Things surgeons can transplant.Cornea: Cornea transplants need no blood-type matching because the cornea has no blood vessels to cause rejection.
Things surgeons can transplant.Pancreas: Pancreas transplants are often done together with a kidney for diabetic patients with kidney failure.
Things surgeons can transplant.Bone marrow: A bone marrow transplant replaces blood-forming stem cells, and it can cure certain leukemias.
Things surgeons can transplant.Skin: Skin grafts help burn victims, sometimes using the patient's own skin taken from another part of the body.
Things surgeons can transplant.Small intestine: Small intestine transplants are rare and reserved for patients whose own guts have failed.
Things surgeons can transplant.Hand: The first hand transplant was attempted in Lyon, France, in 1998, and later ones have lasted for years.
Things surgeons can transplant.Face: The first partial face transplant happened in France in 2005, replacing nose, lips and chin tissue.
Things surgeons can transplant.Hair: Hair transplants move follicles from the back of the head, which resists balding, to thinning areas.
Things surgeons can transplant.Brain: A trap: the brain cannot be transplanted, because its billions of nerve connections cannot be rejoined.
Things surgeons can transplant.Spinal cord: A trap: spinal cords cannot be transplanted, since severed nerve fibers do not reconnect that way.
Things surgeons can transplant.Memories: A trap: memories are stored as networks of connections in the brain, so they cannot be moved between people.
Things surgeons can transplant.Shadow: A trap: a shadow is just an absence of light, not a body part, so no surgeon could ever move it.
Things surgeons can transplant.Reflection: A trap: a reflection is only an image, not tissue, so it cannot be transplanted by any surgeon.
Things surgeons can transplant.Accent: A trap: an accent comes from learning to speak in a certain community, not from tissue you could transplant.
Things surgeons can transplant.Personality: A trap: personality is not an organ, whatever the folklore about heart-transplant recipients claims.
Things surgeons can transplant.Dreams: A trap: dreams happen inside the brain, so there is nothing a surgeon could cut out and move.
Things surgeons can transplant.Laughter: A trap: laughter is an action, not a body part, so there is nothing to transplant from one person to another.
Things surgeons can transplant.Sense of humor: A trap: a sense of humor is not an organ, so it cannot be transplanted between people.
Things surgeons can transplant.Habits: A trap: habits are learned patterns stored in the brain, not tissue that a surgeon could move.
Things surgeons can transplant.Handwriting: A trap: handwriting is a skill held in the brain, so a transplanted hand writes as its new owner's brain directs.

Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Coconut: The brown fibre on a coconut husk is coir, used for doormats and ropes; the husk is the hairy part.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Kiwi fruit: Kiwi fruit was originally called Chinese gooseberry; it was renamed after New Zealand's fuzzy brown kiwi bird.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Peach: A peach's fuzz is made of tiny hairs that may help protect the fruit from insects and moisture; nectarines are just fuzz-free peaches.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Tarantula: A tarantula's hairs can be flicked off at predators, and the barbs itch painfully in the skin and eyes.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Bumblebee: Bumblebees' fuzz traps heat, and by shivering their flight muscles they stay warm enough to forage in cold weather.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Yak: Yaks live at altitudes above 4,000 metres, and their long shaggy coats and huge lungs protect them from extreme cold.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Yeti: The Yeti is the legendary shaggy 'Abominable Snowman' of the Himalayas; scientific tests of supposed relics showed bear DNA.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Tennis ball: A tennis ball's felt covering isn't just for show; it slows the ball in the air, so a bare rubber ball would fly differently.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Teddy bear: The teddy bear is named for US President Theodore Roosevelt, after a famous 1902 hunting trip where he refused to shoot a bear.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Gorilla: Gorillas have coarse hair over most of the body, but adult males develop a silver back, giving the species silverbacks.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Sheep: A sheep's wool keeps growing, and a Merino can produce a fleece weighing several kilos each year.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Llama: Llamas have dense wool that is low in lanolin, and they use a distinctive hum to communicate with their young.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Egg: A trap: an egg has a smooth shell and is neither hairy nor fuzzy, despite chicks hatching from it fluffy.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Apple: Apples have smooth waxy skin; they float because about a quarter of their volume is air.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Snake: Snakes are covered in smooth scales, and they shed their whole outer skin in one piece as they grow.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Goldfish: Goldfish have smooth scales, not fur; they can see more colours than people, including ultraviolet.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Banana: Bananas have smooth peel; the fruit is a berry in botanical terms, and the plant is actually a giant herb.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Frog: Frogs have smooth, moist skin they can partly breathe through, with no hair at all.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Dolphin: Dolphins are mammals but nearly hairless; newborns have a few whiskers on the snout that fall out soon after birth.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Eggplant: Eggplant skin is smooth and glossy, even though the plant's leaves and stems can be somewhat prickly and hairy.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Plum: A plum has smooth skin with a powdery bloom, a natural wax that protects it, not fuzz.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Lizard: Lizards are scaly, not hairy; some, like geckos, climb walls with microscopic hair-like structures on their toes.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Jellyfish: Jellyfish are soft and smooth and have no hair; their bodies are around 95 percent water.
Things that are hairy or fuzzy.Turtle: A turtle's shell is hard, not furry; the shell is part of its skeleton, so it can't ever leave it.

Jobs that work closely with animals.Vet: Vets treat species from hamsters to horses, and a vet may need to adapt to species that can't say where it hurts.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Zookeeper: Zookeepers feed, clean and train animals, and many spend years working on conservation breeding to save endangered species.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Farrier: A farrier trims and shoes horses' hooves, a craft over 2,000 years old, and a good one needs to be both smith and animal handler.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Jockey: Jockeys race horses at about 60 kilometres per hour, often weighing barely more than a child.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Shepherd: Shepherds guide flocks, and in many places they use trained herding dogs, which can do the work of several people.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Dog walker: Dog walkers are paid to exercise others' pets, and in cities the business has grown into a big part of the pet economy.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Pet groomer: Pet groomers trim and bathe animals, and for some breeds, like poodles, the cut is a matter of show-ring tradition.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Beekeeper: Beekeepers look after hives, and a single colony can hold tens of thousands of bees, with just one queen.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Horse trainer: Horse trainers teach horses to carry riders or race, and good ones rely on patience and body language, not force.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Falconer: Falconers train birds of prey to hunt, an art practised for thousands of years, and recognised by UNESCO as cultural heritage.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Lion tamer: Lion tamers perform with big cats, and the job is now rarer, as many countries restrict wild animals in circuses.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Dairy farmer: Dairy farmers care for cows, and a single cow can produce well over 20 litres of milk a day.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Notary: Notaries certify legal documents, a role that comes from ancient Rome, and deals with paper, not pets.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Actuary: Actuaries calculate risk for insurers using statistics, so they work with numbers, not animals.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Cartographer: Cartographers make maps, and the oldest known world maps date back thousands of years, but they don't need animals.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Architect: Architects design buildings. A few specialise in zoos or stables, but most spend their days on plans.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Typist: Typists type documents, a job that fell sharply as computers arrived, and it has no animal side.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Stenographer: Stenographers record speech in shorthand, for example in courts, and need fast fingers, not animal skills.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Locksmith: Locksmiths work with locks and keys, and the oldest known lock is some 4,000 years old, from the Near East.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Upholsterer: Upholsterers cover furniture with fabric and padding, though older padding was often horsehair, which is the nearest link.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Cobbler: Cobblers repair shoes. The leather comes from animals, but the cobbler works with it, not the living animal.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Tailor: Tailors make clothes, and wool is from sheep, but a tailor never meets the animals themselves.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Accountant: Accountants keep financial records, and they work with figures, not with livestock, though some farm accountants might.
Jobs that work closely with animals.Glazier: Glaziers fit glass into windows, and the work is as old as stained glass in medieval churches, with no animals.

Parts of an airplane.Fuselage: The fuselage is the plane's main body, and the word comes from the French for spindle-shaped.
Parts of an airplane.Wing: A wing creates lift because it's shaped so that air passes faster over the top, and the pressure difference pushes the plane up.
Parts of an airplane.Cockpit: The word cockpit originally meant an arena for cockfights, and was applied to a small space in a ship before aircraft.
Parts of an airplane.Tail fin: The tail fin, or vertical stabilizer, keeps a plane from swinging side to side like a weathervane.
Parts of an airplane.Aileron: Ailerons sit on the back of wings, and moving them in opposite directions makes the plane roll to turn.
Parts of an airplane.Landing gear: Many planes tuck their landing gear away after takeoff, to cut the drag that would slow them.
Parts of an airplane.Flaps: Flaps extend from the wings on landing and takeoff, adding lift at low speed, so the plane can fly slower.
Parts of an airplane.Jet engine: A jet engine sucks in air, compresses it, burns fuel in it and shoots the hot gas out the back, producing thrust.
Parts of an airplane.Winglet: Winglets reduce the swirling vortices at the wing tip, which can save a few percent of fuel on a long flight.
Parts of an airplane.Elevator: The elevator on the tail pitches the nose up and down, and has nothing to do with a lift in a building.
Parts of an airplane.Rudder: A rudder on a plane's tail swings the nose left or right, and it's a feature that planes and ships share.
Parts of an airplane.Nose cone: The nose cone, or radome, houses the weather radar, and is made of a material the radar can see through.
Parts of an airplane.Keel: A keel is a ship's backbone, and while some flying boats had hulls, a typical airplane has none.
Parts of an airplane.Mast: A mast holds sails or antennas on a ship, and is not a part of an airplane.
Parts of an airplane.Bilge: The bilge is where water collects at a ship's bottom, a boat word unrelated to planes.
Parts of an airplane.Poop deck: The poop deck is the raised deck at the stern, and the name comes from the Latin puppis, meaning stern, and not from any rude word.
Parts of an airplane.Crow's nest: The crow's nest was a ship's lookout perch, high on the mast, and planes use the cockpit instead.
Parts of an airplane.Paddle wheel: Paddle wheels drove Mississippi steamboats, powered by steam, and have no place on an airplane.
Parts of an airplane.Gangplank: A gangplank is a ramp for boarding a ship, while planes use airstairs or jet bridges.
Parts of an airplane.Rigging: Rigging is the ropes and chains that support a ship's masts and sails, though some early aircraft also used wires named rigging.
Parts of an airplane.Sail: Sails catch the wind to move a ship, and the trap is that planes' wings also work with air, but they use lift.
Parts of an airplane.Bowsprit: The bowsprit is the pole poking out from the front of a sailing ship, to hold the forward sails.
Parts of an airplane.Figurehead: Figureheads were carved statues on a ship's bow, believed to guard against storms and be the ship's spirit.
Parts of an airplane.Oar: Oars are used to row boats, and the rowing galleys of ancient times were powered by many men pulling together.

People who work on a farm.Farmhand: Hired labourers do everything from milking to harvest, and many farms still rely on seasonal help in busy weeks.
People who work on a farm.Shepherd: In the Alps, shepherds move flocks to high pastures each summer in a seasonal move called transhumance.
People who work on a farm.Milkmaid: Edward Jenner noticed milkmaids who caught cowpox seemed protected from smallpox, leading to vaccination in 1796.
People who work on a farm.Tractor driver: Modern tractors use GPS auto-steer to plough rows accurate to within a few centimetres.
People who work on a farm.Herdsman: Sámi herders in northern Europe still follow reindeer herds across the seasons.
People who work on a farm.Fruit picker: Apple pickers twist rather than pull, so the stem stays on and the fruit keeps longer.
People who work on a farm.Cowhand: Cowhands drove Texas cattle up trails to Kansas railheads in the 1860s and 1870s.
People who work on a farm.Stable hand: Mucks out stalls, feeds and grooms horses; racing stables start before dawn.
People who work on a farm.Dairy farmer: A dairy cow gives roughly 25 litres of milk a day, but only after having a calf.
People who work on a farm.Sheep shearer: A skilled shearer can remove a fleece in a couple of minutes, and record-setters shear hundreds in a day.
People who work on a farm.Ranch hand: Works a large livestock spread; Texas's King Ranch is bigger than the state of Rhode Island.
People who work on a farm.Bellhop: Carries luggage at a hotel; the term comes from guests ringing a bell for them.
People who work on a farm.Croupier: Runs casino tables like roulette, where the wheel has 37 or 38 pockets.
People who work on a farm.Bailiff: Keeps order in court, but in medieval England a bailiff also managed a lord's estate, so the word once had a farm link.
People who work on a farm.Usher: Seats guests at theatres and weddings; the word began as a doorkeeper, so the job is still about entrances.
People who work on a farm.Sommelier: Serves and advises on wine; farmers grow the grapes, but the sommelier works in the restaurant.
People who work on a farm.Stockbroker: Trades shares on the stock market; 'stock' also means livestock, which is why this one trips people.
People who work on a farm.Flight attendant: Serves and secures passengers in the air; a certified safety role first, service second.
People who work on a farm.Lifeguard: Watches swimmers at pools and beaches; on a farm, the pond is rarely supervised.
People who work on a farm.Librarian: Manages books and information; Melvil Dewey's decimal system from 1876 still organises many libraries.
People who work on a farm.Barista: Italian for bartender; a coffee-making role, and coffee is grown on farms far from most baristas.
People who work on a farm.Dentist: Cares for teeth; livestock teeth are handled by a large-animal vet instead.
People who work on a farm.Gondolier: Steers Venetian gondolas, a waterborne trade rather than a pastoral one.
People who work on a farm.Astronaut: Flies in space, not a farm job, though astronauts have grown lettuce on the International Space Station.

Things a greengrocer sells.Apples: There are over 7,500 apple varieties in the world, yet a supermarket may stock just a handful, which a greengrocer can beat.
Things a greengrocer sells.Carrots: Early carrots were purple and yellow; the familiar orange kind was developed in the Netherlands in the 1600s.
Things a greengrocer sells.Potatoes: Potatoes were domesticated in the Andes thousands of years ago, and there are thousands of varieties there, in many colors.
Things a greengrocer sells.Lettuce: It is about 95 percent water, and its Latin name Lactuca comes from the milky sap that oozes when it is cut.
Things a greengrocer sells.Bananas: Bananas are technically berries, and the common Cavendish variety is a clone, so every banana is genetically almost identical.
Things a greengrocer sells.Onions: They make us cry because cutting releases a gas that mixes with the moisture of the eye to form a mild sulfur acid.
Things a greengrocer sells.Tomatoes: Botanically a fruit, tomatoes were once feared in Europe as poisonous, partly because they belong to the nightshade family.
Things a greengrocer sells.Leeks: Leeks are the national emblem of Wales, and legend says Welsh soldiers wore them in a battle to tell friend from foe.
Things a greengrocer sells.Cabbage: Cabbage is the ancestor of broccoli, cauliflower, kale and Brussels sprouts, all bred from one wild plant.
Things a greengrocer sells.Oranges: The color orange was named after the fruit, not the other way around, and before that English speakers called it yellow-red.
Things a greengrocer sells.Mushrooms: Mushrooms are closer to animals than plants in their family tree, and they make vitamin D when exposed to sunlight.
Things a greengrocer sells.Sausages: A butcher's job, not a greengrocer's; the word comes from Latin for salted, as the meat was preserved with salt.
