Things a greengrocer sells.Bread: A baker's product, and the word "companion" means someone you share bread with, from the Latin for "with bread".
Things a greengrocer sells.Cheese: A dairy or deli item; cheese is one of the oldest foods, and traces of it have been found in 3,000-year-old Egyptian tombs.
Things a greengrocer sells.Milk: It's a dairy product, and in the past milkmen delivered bottles to doorsteps at dawn, with no greengrocer involved.
Things a greengrocer sells.Nails: Hardware stores sell nails, and the units for them, "penny", are said to come from old prices per hundred.
Things a greengrocer sells.Newspapers: Newsagents sell them, and the oldest still-printed ones go back to the 1600s.
Things a greengrocer sells.Steak: A butcher's cut; the word is from Old Norse for roast on a stick, and no vegetable shop sells it.
Things a greengrocer sells.Chicken: Chickens are thought to descend from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia, and a butcher, not a greengrocer, stocks them.
Things a greengrocer sells.Fish: Fishmongers sell fish, and the profession is old enough to have a medieval London guild, the Fishmongers' Company.
Things a greengrocer sells.Cake: A bakery item; the word comes from Old Norse "kaka", and early cakes were more like sweetened bread.
Things a greengrocer sells.Shampoo: It comes from the Hindi word "champo", meaning to massage, and sells in pharmacies, not at the vegetable stall.
Things a greengrocer sells.Batteries: A hardware or electrical shop sells them, and Benjamin Franklin popularized the word for a linked set of charged jars.
Things a greengrocer sells.Stamps: The first adhesive postage stamp was the British Penny Black of 1840, and it is bought at a post office.

Networking hardware.Router: Your home router is a small computer running its own operating system, often Linux, and it needs regular firmware updates for security.
Networking hardware.Modem: The name blends modulator and demodulator: it turns digital data into signals a phone, cable or fiber line can carry, and back again.
Networking hardware.Network switch: Unlike a hub, a switch learns which device sits on which port and sends data only where it's needed, so traffic doesn't collide.
Networking hardware.Hub: Hubs repeat every incoming signal out of every port, which made busy networks slow; switches have almost entirely replaced them.
Networking hardware.Access point: It bridges wireless devices onto a wired network. Offices often install many, so your phone hands off between them as you walk.
Networking hardware.Wi-Fi extender: Most extenders must receive and rebroadcast on the same radio, which can roughly halve your speed. Mesh systems avoid this.
Networking hardware.Ethernet cable: Twisted pairs of wires inside cancel out electrical noise. The twist is why Cat5, Cat6 and friends work at all over long runs.
Networking hardware.Network card: Every network card has a unique MAC address burned in at the factory, with the first half identifying the manufacturer.
Networking hardware.Patch panel: This wall of ports in server closets lets technicians re-route connections with short cables instead of rewiring the building.
Networking hardware.Monitor: A monitor only displays what a computer sends it. It's an output device, not part of the network gear that moves data around.
Networking hardware.Printer: It can sit on a network, but it's an endpoint that receives jobs rather than hardware that carries traffic between devices.
Networking hardware.Mouse: Douglas Engelbart's first mouse in the 1960s was a wooden block with wheels. It is an input device, not network gear.
Networking hardware.Keyboard: The QWERTY layout is far older than computers; it's an input device and plays no part in moving network traffic.
Networking hardware.Webcam: The first webcam famously watched a coffee pot at Cambridge University in 1991. It's an input device, not networking gear.
Networking hardware.Scanner: Scanners digitize paper into files. Even when plugged into a network they're a source of data, not a carrier of it.
Networking hardware.Speakers: Speakers are output devices that turn electrical signals into sound; they may stream over Wi-Fi but don't route anything.
Networking hardware.Joystick: Joysticks began as aircraft control sticks and migrated to games. They send input to a computer, never network traffic.
Networking hardware.Graphics card: It's easy to confuse with a network card since both are expansion cards, but this one renders images, not packets.
Networking hardware.Sound card: Another expansion card that sounds networky, yet it only converts audio between digital and analog forms.
Networking hardware.Hard drive: Storage can be shared across a network, but a bare hard drive only holds data; it doesn't route or connect anything.
Networking hardware.Trackpad: Trackpads sense finger position by measuring tiny changes in electrical capacitance. They're pointing devices, not network gear.
Networking hardware.Stylus: A stylus is a pointing tool for touchscreens and tablets, so it belongs with input devices rather than networking.
Networking hardware.Microphone: Microphones feed sound into a computer. Voice calls travel over networks, but the mic itself isn't network hardware.
Networking hardware.Projector: A projector only shows an image from a source. Some connect via Wi-Fi, but that makes them clients, not infrastructure.

Street Fighter characters.Ryu: The series' wandering martial-arts hero is famous for the Hadouken fireball and the Shoryuken uppercut.
Street Fighter characters.Ken: Ryu's blond, American-born training partner; in the early games he was nearly a palette-swapped clone of Ryu.
Street Fighter characters.Chun-Li: An Interpol officer who debuted in Street Fighter II in 1991, often called the first major female fighter in fighting games.
Street Fighter characters.Guile: A US Air Force fighter with a gravity-defying flat-top, known for his Sonic Boom and a theme song players say goes with everything.
Street Fighter characters.Blanka: A green, electric beast from Brazil; the lore says his skin turned green from chlorophyll after he was raised in the jungle.
Street Fighter characters.Zangief: A Soviet wrestler known as the Red Cyclone, famous for his Spinning Piledriver and for wrestling bears, as the lore goes.
Street Fighter characters.Dhalsim: A yoga master from India whose limbs stretch and who breathes fire, fighting to feed his village rather than for glory.
Street Fighter characters.E. Honda: A sumo wrestler from Japan known for his Hundred Hand Slap; the E in his name stands for Edmond.
Street Fighter characters.M. Bison: The dictator who leads Shadaloo is the main villain; in Japan, names were shuffled and he's called Vega there.
Street Fighter characters.Vega: The claw-wielding Spanish bullfighter is vain about his looks; in Japanese versions he goes by the name Balrog.
Street Fighter characters.Sagat: The towering Muay Thai champion carries a scar from Ryu's Shoryuken and was the final boss of the original Street Fighter.
Street Fighter characters.Balrog: A heavyweight boxer widely seen as a nod to Mike Tyson; in Japan, his name is M. Bison.
Street Fighter characters.Cammy: A British Delta Red agent introduced in Super Street Fighter II in 1993, famous for her spiral Cannon Spike kick.
Street Fighter characters.Scorpion: A trap: Scorpion is a ninja from Mortal Kombat, the rival fighting series, known for his shout of 'Get over here!'
Street Fighter characters.Sub-Zero: The ice ninja of Mortal Kombat, a rival series. Two different brothers have worn the name over the years.
Street Fighter characters.Raiden: The thunder god and protector of Earthrealm in Mortal Kombat, so he belongs to the rival series.
Street Fighter characters.Liu Kang: A Shaolin monk and tournament champion in Mortal Kombat, one of its most frequent heroes. Not Street Fighter.
Street Fighter characters.Sonya Blade: A US Special Forces officer, one of Mortal Kombat's original 1992 characters, so she's from the other series.
Street Fighter characters.Kitana: The princess of Edenia armed with razor-edged steel fans, a Mortal Kombat fighter and not part of Street Fighter's cast.
Street Fighter characters.Johnny Cage: A movie star turned fighter in Mortal Kombat, known for his sunglasses and reportedly inspired by Jean-Claude Van Damme.
Street Fighter characters.Goro: A four-armed Shokan boss in the first Mortal Kombat, animated from a sculpted clay model. He belongs to the rival series.
Street Fighter characters.Shang Tsung: A soul-stealing sorcerer who hosts the Mortal Kombat tournament and can shapeshift into other fighters.
Street Fighter characters.Jax: Major Jackson Briggs, a Special Forces officer with metal arms, who joined Mortal Kombat II as a Mortal Kombat regular.
Street Fighter characters.Mileena: Kitana's toothy clone armed with sai, introduced in Mortal Kombat II, so a Mortal Kombat fighter.

Jobs in a theater production.Director: The person who shapes the production's overall vision, but the role is fairly modern; actor-managers ran shows until the late 1800s.
Jobs in a theater production.Stage manager: Runs the show during performances, calling every light and sound cue from the prompt book, and has more control than the director once the curtain rises.
Jobs in a theater production.Usher: Seats the audience and handles the house, from a French word meaning doorkeeper.
Jobs in a theater production.Understudy: Learns a role in case the principal is ill; some actors have waited years for their night, and many have stepped in with minutes' notice.
Jobs in a theater production.Lighting designer: Designs how the stage looks and feels, and in the 1880s the switch from gas to electric lights transformed theatre.
Jobs in a theater production.Prompter: Sits in the wings or in a box, feeding lines to actors who forget them, which is an older tradition than most.
Jobs in a theater production.Stagehand: Shifts scenery and props in the dark, and the term is related to a long tradition of sailors working theatre rigging.
Jobs in a theater production.Choreographer: Designs the dance and movement in a show; in musicals this role can be as important as the composer.
Jobs in a theater production.Costume designer: Creates what the characters wear and often works with period research, fabric and fast-change engineering.
Jobs in a theater production.Dramaturg: A literary adviser who researches the play and its context; the job began in 18th-century Germany with Lessing.
Jobs in a theater production.Set designer: Builds the world of the play; early Renaissance designers used painted perspective scenery to fake depth.
Jobs in a theater production.Umpire: A sports official who judges play in tennis, baseball or cricket, rather than managing a stage.
Jobs in a theater production.Referee: A sports official who enforces the rules of a game, as in football, which has a famous whistle.
Jobs in a theater production.Caddie: Carries a golfer's clubs and offers advice; the word comes from "cadet", via Mary, Queen of Scots.
Jobs in a theater production.Sommelier: A wine steward in a restaurant, from an old French word for a pack-animal driver.
Jobs in a theater production.Barista: The Italian word for a bartender, now a coffee-making specialist.
Jobs in a theater production.Lifeguard: Watches over swimmers from a high chair, and the lifeguard's red-and-yellow flag system is used on many beaches worldwide.
Jobs in a theater production.Cartographer: Makes maps; the term comes from Latin for "chart" and "write".
Jobs in a theater production.Midwife: Helps with birth; the word comes from Old English for "with woman".
Jobs in a theater production.Plumber: Named after the Latin for lead, plumbum, which Romans used for pipes.
Jobs in a theater production.Jockey: Rides racehorses at speeds near 40 mph, and weighs little over 110 pounds, so many jockeys fast or sweat to stay light.
Jobs in a theater production.Astronaut: Travels beyond Earth's atmosphere; the term comes from Greek for "star sailor".
Jobs in a theater production.Goalkeeper: The only football player permitted to use their hands on the pitch, not on a stage.
Jobs in a theater production.Lumberjack: Fells trees for timber, a job far from the theatre and its tools.

Animals Aesop could have written about.Tortoise: In Aesop's race, slow and steady beats a boastful rival; Greek tortoise fables date to about the sixth century BC.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Hare: The overconfident hare naps mid-race and loses to the tortoise; the fable has been retold for over two thousand years.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Fox: Aesop's fox, unable to reach the grapes, calls them sour; that gave us the phrase 'sour grapes'.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Crow: In the fable of the thirsty crow, it drops pebbles into a pitcher to raise the water, and real crows can do this trick.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Ant: In Aesop's tale, the hardworking ant stores food all summer, and it makes the grasshopper's winter hunger a lesson in planning.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Grasshopper: Aesop's careless musician fiddles away summer and begs for food in winter; in some versions it is a cicada.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Lion: In the fable of the lion and the mouse, a tiny mouse frees the king of beasts from a hunter's net by gnawing the ropes.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Mouse: The mouse that gnaws the lion's net shows Aesop's lesson that even the weak can repay a kindness.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Wolf: Aesop's 'boy who cried wolf' made the false-alarm lesson famous, and the wolf also appears as a bully in the lamb tales.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Lamb: In the wolf-and-lamb fable the wolf invents excuses to eat the lamb anyway, because 'any excuse will serve a tyrant'.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Stork: Aesop's stork gets caught among the cranes by a farmer's net, and the lesson is that you are judged by your company.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Goose: The goose that laid golden eggs ended up dead when its greedy owner cut it open, which is where 'killing the golden goose' comes from.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Penguin: Penguins live only in the Southern Hemisphere, far from ancient Greece, so Aesop never knew of one.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Kangaroo: Aesop wrote in ancient Greece, and kangaroos live only in Australia, which Europeans did not reach until the 1600s.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Panda: Giant pandas were unknown outside China to the West until 1869, many centuries after Aesop.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Llama: Llamas are South American animals; the Greeks of Aesop's day had never heard of them.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Koala: Koalas live only in eastern Australia and sleep up to about 20 hours a day, far from Aesop's Mediterranean.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Platypus: Europeans first saw the egg-laying platypus in 1798, and early scientists suspected a hoax stitched from different animals.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Armadillo: Armadillos are New World animals, so no ancient Greek storyteller could have used one.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Sloth: Sloths are only in Central and South America, so they missed Aesop's menagerie.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Raccoon: Raccoons are North American natives, unknown in ancient Greece, so Aesop never told a tale about one.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Turkey: Turkeys come from the Americas and reached Europe only after Columbus, nearly two thousand years after Aesop.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Hummingbird: Hummingbirds live only in the Americas, so Aesop could not have known them; they are the only birds that can fly backward.
Animals Aesop could have written about.Jaguar: The jaguar is the biggest cat of the Americas and was unknown to the ancient Greeks.

Metals.Gold: All the gold ever mined would fit in a cube roughly 22 meters on a side.
Metals.Iron: Iron makes up most of Earth's core, and it's the most common element on the planet by mass.
Metals.Copper: Copper kills germs on contact, so hospitals use it for door handles and rails.
Metals.Aluminum: Aluminum was once rarer than gold, and Napoleon III reportedly served honored guests with aluminum cutlery.
Metals.Mercury: Mercury's chemical symbol Hg comes from the Latin hydrargyrum, meaning liquid silver.
Metals.Zinc: Zinc coats steel in a process called galvanizing, sacrificing itself to prevent rust.
Metals.Tin: A tin can is mostly steel with a thin coating of tin.
Metals.Lead: The Latin name for lead, plumbum, is the source of the word plumber, since Romans piped water through it.
Metals.Silver: Silver's chemical symbol Ag comes from argentum, which gave Argentina its name.
Metals.Titanium: Titanium is as strong as steel at about 45 percent less weight, and the human body tolerates it well.
Metals.Nickel: The US five-cent nickel is actually 75 percent copper and just 25 percent nickel.
Metals.Platinum: Platinum is rarer than gold, and Spanish conquistadors dismissed it as platina, little silver.
Metals.Sodium: Sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water, and table salt is sodium combined with chlorine.
Metals.Carbon: Carbon is a nonmetal, yet graphite conducts electricity like a metal.
Metals.Sulfur: Sulfur is a yellow nonmetal, and the rotten egg smell comes from hydrogen sulfide.
Metals.Oxygen: Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust by mass, but it's a gas.
Metals.Glass: Plain glass is mostly silica from sand, with no metal to speak of.
Metals.Plastic: Most plastics are long chains of carbon, which makes them nonmetals through and through.
Metals.Granite: Granite is a rock made of quartz, feldspar and mica; it contains metals chemically, but isn't one.
Metals.Diamond: Diamond is pure carbon and nothing like a metal.
Metals.Graphite: Pencil lead has no lead in it; it's graphite, a form of carbon.
Metals.Helium: Helium is a noble gas that's famously inert.
Metals.Quartz: Quartz is silicon dioxide, used in watches because it vibrates at a very steady rate.
Metals.Iodine: Iodine is a nonmetal, a purple-black solid, and your thyroid needs it.

Natural fibers.Cotton: Cotton fiber is the fluff around the plant's seeds and is nearly pure cellulose.
Natural fibers.Wool: Lanolin, the grease in sheep's wool, ends up in lip balms and skin creams.
Natural fibers.Silk: China kept silk-making secret for thousands of years, until the knowledge spread along the Silk Road.
Natural fibers.Linen: Linen is made from flax, one of the oldest textiles, and it wrapped Egyptian mummies.
Natural fibers.Hemp: Hemp fiber was used for ship sails and ropes, and the word canvas comes from cannabis.
Natural fibers.Cashmere: Cashmere is named for the Kashmir region and combed from the soft undercoat of goats rather than sheared.
Natural fibers.Alpaca: Alpaca fleece contains no lanolin, which makes it a favorite for people sensitive to wool.
Natural fibers.Mohair: Mohair comes from Angora goats, not Angora rabbits.
Natural fibers.Jute: Angora comes from the Angora rabbit and is named for Ankara, once known as Angora.
Natural fibers.Angora: Jute, grown largely in Bengal, is sometimes called the golden fiber and is used for burlap.
Natural fibers.Sisal: Sisal comes from agave leaves and is used in rope, dartboards and cat scratching posts.
Natural fibers.Camel hair: Camels shed their soft undercoat each spring, and it's collected for classic coats.
Natural fibers.Polyester: Polyester is a petroleum-based plastic and the most widely used fiber in the world.
Natural fibers.Nylon: Nylon was the first fully synthetic fiber, introduced by DuPont in 1935 and sold as stockings in 1940.
Natural fibers.Acrylic: Acrylic is a synthetic fiber designed to mimic wool.
Natural fibers.Spandex: Spandex can stretch to about five times its length, and was invented in 1958 by Joseph Shivers at DuPont.
Natural fibers.Kevlar: Kevlar is five times stronger than steel by weight, and it's what bulletproof vests are made of.
Natural fibers.Lycra: Lycra is a brand name for spandex, not a natural fiber.
Natural fibers.Polypropylene: Polypropylene wicks moisture away from skin, which is why it's common in thermal underwear.
Natural fibers.Fiberglass: Fiberglass is glass spun into thread, a manufactured fiber, not a natural one.
Natural fibers.Microfiber: Microfiber is typically polyester and nylon with strands finer than a silk thread.
Natural fibers.Vinyl: Vinyl is PVC, used for records and siding, and it's thoroughly synthetic.
Natural fibers.Neoprene: Neoprene was invented by DuPont in 1930 as a synthetic rubber, and it's what wetsuits are made of.
Natural fibers.Gore-Tex: Gore-Tex membrane pores are smaller than water drops but larger than vapor molecules, so sweat escapes while rain stays out.

Things traditionally made of leather.Baseball glove: Baseball gloves are leather, usually cowhide, and a new one is often broken in with oil and a ball tied inside.
Things traditionally made of leather.Horse saddle: Saddles have been made of leather for centuries, and a good one can last for generations with care.
Things traditionally made of leather.Cowboy boots: Cowboy boots have a tall shaft and angled heel designed to keep a rider's foot in the stirrup.
Things traditionally made of leather.Lederhosen: Lederhosen are Bavarian leather shorts, and the name literally means 'leather trousers' in German.
Things traditionally made of leather.Bullwhip: A bullwhip's crack is a tiny sonic boom, because the tip moves faster than the speed of sound.
Things traditionally made of leather.Bridle: A bridle is a leather headpiece that holds the bit and reins, and its design has changed little in centuries.
Things traditionally made of leather.NFL football: The NFL ball is nicknamed 'the pigskin,' though it's now made of cowhide, and it was once a pig's inflated bladder.
Things traditionally made of leather.Biker jacket: Biker jackets are leather for abrasion resistance, and the style was popularized by 1950s movies and rock stars.
Things traditionally made of leather.Holster: Holsters are typically leather, which is stiff enough to hold a gun's shape and quiet when drawn.
Things traditionally made of leather.Baseball: A baseball's cover is stitched from cowhide with 108 red stitches, and it wraps around a cork-and-rubber core.
Things traditionally made of leather.Flip-flops: Flip-flops are typically rubber or foam, and sandals like them date back thousands of years in Egypt.
Things traditionally made of leather.Rain boots: Rain boots are usually rubber, a material that waterproofs where leather would soak through and stiffen.
Things traditionally made of leather.Wool sweater: Wool comes from sheep fleece rather than hide, and its crimped fibers trap air to hold warmth.
Things traditionally made of leather.Raincoat: Raincoats are made of waterproof fabrics or coated nylon, because leather soaks up water and stiffens.
Things traditionally made of leather.Tennis ball: A tennis ball is rubber covered in felt, and the fuzz slows it down and affects how it flies.
Things traditionally made of leather.Golf ball: A golf ball has dimples that reduce drag so it flies farther, and its cover is plastic or urethane.
Things traditionally made of leather.Hockey puck: A hockey puck is vulcanized rubber, and its hard dense material lets it slide quickly across ice.
Things traditionally made of leather.Beach ball: A beach ball is inflatable vinyl, which is made to be light and bounce on water.
Things traditionally made of leather.Bowling ball: Bowling balls are made of polyurethane, plastic, or resin, and the finger holes are drilled to fit each bowler.
Things traditionally made of leather.Swimsuit: Swimsuits are stretchy synthetic fabrics like nylon, and some competition suits are banned for giving too much buoyancy.
Things traditionally made of leather.Umbrella: Umbrella canopies are waterproof fabric like nylon or polyester, because leather would be heavy and stiff.
Things traditionally made of leather.Fleece jacket: Fleece is a synthetic fabric typically made from polyester, and some are made from recycled plastic bottles.
Things traditionally made of leather.Shower cap: Shower caps are made of plastic or vinyl with elastic edges to keep water out, not leather.
Things traditionally made of leather.Wetsuit: A wetsuit is neoprene, a foam rubber that traps a thin layer of water your body warms up.

Things you find at an airport.Runway: Runways are numbered by compass heading, so runway 27 points to roughly 270 degrees, due west.
Things you find at an airport.Terminal: Terminal buildings gather check-in, security, shops, and gates, and some, like Beijing Daxing's, are among the world's largest buildings.
Things you find at an airport.Gate: Gate numbers are assigned by airlines and airports, and at very large airports, passengers sometimes need to ride a train between gates.
Things you find at an airport.Control tower: Air traffic controllers in the tower can see the whole airfield, and tower glass is tilted to cut glare.
Things you find at an airport.Baggage claim: Checked bags are tagged with a three-letter airport code, and the carousel is a continuous belt that loops.
Things you find at an airport.Customs: Customs officers check what travelers bring across borders, and agricultural rules often ban fresh fruit and meat.
Things you find at an airport.Departure board: Old airport departure boards used flipping mechanical letters, and their clatter was once the sound of travel.
Things you find at an airport.Hangar: A hangar shelters aircraft for maintenance, and the word comes from an old French term for a shed.
Things you find at an airport.Jet bridge: The jet bridge, or jetway, is a movable tube linking the gate to the plane's door, and it lets passengers board without going outside.
Things you find at an airport.Duty-free shop: Duty-free shops sell goods without local taxes, and the first one opened at Shannon Airport, Ireland, in 1947.
Things you find at an airport.Security scanner: Airport body scanners use millimeter waves or X-rays to detect hidden objects without a pat-down.
Things you find at an airport.Boarding pass: A boarding pass's barcode holds your name, flight, and seat, and many airlines now offer it only on your phone.
Things you find at an airport.Windsock: A windsock shows wind direction and rough speed to pilots, and it's fully extended when winds hit about 15 knots.
Things you find at an airport.Lighthouse: A lighthouse guides ships at sea, not planes; the world's tallest stands in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and is about 133 meters.
Things you find at an airport.Pier: A pier juts into water for ships and fishing and not planes, though some airports were built on land reclaimed from the sea.
Things you find at an airport.Caboose: The caboose was a crew car at the end of freight trains, and it's a railroad item that has largely vanished.
Things you find at an airport.Signal box: A signal box houses the railway levers that control trains, and its job parallels an air control tower.
Things you find at an airport.Gangplank: A gangplank is the board used to board a ship, which is similar to a jet bridge, but it belongs at a harbor.
Things you find at an airport.Anchor: An anchor holds a ship in place, and large ones can weigh over 20 tonnes, but airports don't use them.
Things you find at an airport.Drawbridge: A drawbridge lifts to let boats pass or to block castle entrances, but it isn't part of a standard airport.
Things you find at an airport.Moat: A moat is a water-filled ditch around a castle, and it's the old equivalent of airport security.
Things you find at an airport.Haystack: Haystacks store dried grass on farms, and Monet famously painted a series of them in the 1890s, but airports don't have any.
Things you find at an airport.Locomotive: A locomotive pulls trains on rails, and the first public steam railway began in England in 1825.
Things you find at an airport.Paddock: A paddock is a small field for horses, and it's also where racehorses are shown before racing.

Things at a horse racecourse.Jockey: Flat-race jockeys are small, typically weigh about 50-55 kg, and wear the owner's colors in the race.
Things at a horse racecourse.Saddle: A racing saddle weighs under 1 kg, far less than a normal riding saddle, so a horse carries little extra weight.
Things at a horse racecourse.Starting gate: Stalls were introduced in the mid 1900s to give every horse an even break; before that, races started with a flag.
Things at a horse racecourse.Finish post: Close races are decided by a photo finish, in which a camera takes thousands of images per second at the line.
Things at a horse racecourse.Grandstand: The grandstand name comes from the best view of the race; the Grand National at Aintree is named for a grand tradition, not the stands.
Things at a horse racecourse.Paddock: Before each race, horses are paraded here so punters can judge their condition; the same word describes a small field.
Things at a horse racecourse.Bookmaker: Bookmakers set odds and take bets; the term 'bookie' comes from the habit of writing every wager in a book.
Things at a horse racecourse.Silks: The colorful jackets and caps, known as silks, let spectators identify horses at a distance; each owner registers a design.
Things at a horse racecourse.Winner's enclosure: The winning horse is led to a special pen, where jockey, owner and trainer are applauded and the horse is unsaddled.
Things at a horse racecourse.Racecard: This printed program lists each runner, its jockey, weight and form so punters can study before betting.
Things at a horse racecourse.Steward: Racecourse stewards enforce the rules and can disqualify a winner after a stewards' inquiry for interference.
Things at a horse racecourse.Pit lane: A trap: the pit lane is a motor racing feature, where cars stop for tires and fuel. Horses don't make pit stops.
Things at a horse racecourse.Chequered flag: Waved to end a motor race. Horse racing finishes with a post and a photo, not a flag.
Things at a horse racecourse.Safety car: Used in Formula One to slow the field after a crash; horse racing has no equivalent vehicle.
Things at a horse racecourse.Wicket: The wicket is the three stumps and two bails in cricket, and this sport is played on a pitch, not a racecourse.
Things at a horse racecourse.Puck: A hard rubber disc used in ice hockey, which is vulcanized rubber and about 3 inches wide. Not a racecourse item.
Things at a horse racecourse.Hoop: Hoops belong to basketball, where the rim is 10 feet high; at a racecourse you'd see rails, not hoops.
Things at a horse racecourse.Diving board: A pool feature for diving; olympic platforms are 10 m high. Horse racing happens on turf or dirt, not in water.
Things at a horse racecourse.Scrum: A rugby formation where forwards bind together and push for the ball; not a racing term.
Things at a horse racecourse.Caddie: A golfer's bag carrier. A jockey rides a horse alone, with no helper carrying anything along the course.
Things at a horse racecourse.End zone: The scoring area in American football; the field there is 10 yards deep. Racecourses have no such zone.
Things at a horse racecourse.Pit crew: The mechanics who service race cars in seconds; a Formula One tire change can take under 2 seconds. Horses have no pit crew.
Things at a horse racecourse.Shuttlecock: The feathered projectile in badminton, which can leave the racket at over 400 km/h. It is not a racecourse item.
Things at a horse racecourse.Bullpen: The area where baseball relief pitchers warm up; not a racecourse item, even though a bull may be at a rodeo.

Chinese zodiac animals.Rat: The first animal of the cycle: legend says the clever Rat hitched a ride on the Ox's back and jumped ahead to win the Great Race.
Chinese zodiac animals.Ox: Hardworking and steady, the Ox came second in the legend, only because the Rat jumped off its head at the finish line.
Chinese zodiac animals.Tiger: The Tiger symbolizes courage and power; in China its forehead markings resemble the character for king, which is why it is called the king of beasts.
Chinese zodiac animals.Rabbit: Known as the Cat in Vietnam's zodiac, the Rabbit is a symbol of luck and gentleness in much of East Asia.
Chinese zodiac animals.Dragon: The only mythical creature in the cycle, and the Dragon is a symbol of imperial power and good fortune.
Chinese zodiac animals.Snake: Snakes are seen as wise and mysterious in the zodiac, and Year of the Snake falls every 12 years, as in 2025.
Chinese zodiac animals.Horse: The Horse stands for energy and freedom; people born in its year are said to be cheerful and independent.
Chinese zodiac animals.Goat: Also called Sheep or Ram depending on translation; the Chinese word yang covers all of them, so the sign's animal is ambiguous.
Chinese zodiac animals.Monkey: Clever and curious, the Monkey is the ninth animal and is tied to the trickster hero of the novel Journey to the West.
Chinese zodiac animals.Rooster: The only bird in the cycle, and the Rooster is linked to punctuality because it crows at dawn.
Chinese zodiac animals.Dog: The eleventh animal stands for loyalty and honesty, and it came late to the race because it stopped to play in the water.
Chinese zodiac animals.Pig: Last in the Great Race, the Pig is the twelfth sign and is linked to wealth and contentment.
Chinese zodiac animals.Cat: A famous trap: the cat is missing because, in one version of the tale, the Rat tricked it into oversleeping the race.
Chinese zodiac animals.Lion: Lions never appear in the zodiac; the cycle holds only the twelve animals of the legend, none of them a big cat except the Tiger.
Chinese zodiac animals.Elephant: Elephants are not among the twelve, though they are honored in other Asian traditions such as Thailand and India.
Chinese zodiac animals.Bear: Bears have no place in the cycle, even though Western zodiac has the Great Bear constellation.
Chinese zodiac animals.Wolf: Wolves are not zodiac animals; the closest canine is the Dog, the eleventh sign.
Chinese zodiac animals.Fox: Foxes are absent from the Chinese zodiac, though in East Asian folklore they are spirits with many tails.
Chinese zodiac animals.Panda: Giant pandas are a Chinese national symbol, but they never made it into the zodiac's twelve animals.
Chinese zodiac animals.Deer: Deer are linked to longevity in Chinese art, but they are not zodiac signs.
Chinese zodiac animals.Eagle: Eagles don't appear in the Chinese zodiac, where the Rooster is the only bird.
Chinese zodiac animals.Crane: Cranes symbolize long life in China and Japan, yet are not part of the twelve-animal cycle.
Chinese zodiac animals.Turtle: Turtles are among the four benevolent animals in Chinese myth, but they are not zodiac signs.
Chinese zodiac animals.Duck: Ducks, a symbol of fidelity in China, miss out on the zodiac; the Rooster carries the bird slot.

Fictional towns and cities.Gotham: Gotham is Batman's city, and its nickname for New York City dates to Washington Irving in 1807.
Fictional towns and cities.Metropolis: Metropolis is Superman's city, and its name came from Fritz Lang's 1927 film, though the real city is in Illinois.
Fictional towns and cities.Sunnydale: Sunnydale is the California town in Buffy the Vampire Slayer, which sits on a Hellmouth.
Fictional towns and cities.Hill Valley: Hill Valley is the California town in Back to the Future, where a clock tower is struck by lightning.
Fictional towns and cities.Emerald City: Emerald City is Oz's capital, and its green is from the glasses visitors must wear in the book.
Fictional towns and cities.Zootopia: Zootopia is the city of animals in Disney's 2016 film, and a mammal metropolis.
Fictional towns and cities.Bikini Bottom: Bikini Bottom is SpongeBob's undersea town, named for Bikini Atoll, where nuclear tests happened.
Fictional towns and cities.Townsville: Townsville is home to the Powerpuff Girls, a city of crime-fighting kindergartners.
Fictional towns and cities.Quahog: Quahog is the Rhode Island town in Family Guy, named for a hard-shell clam.
Fictional towns and cities.Pawnee: Pawnee is the Indiana town in Parks and Recreation, the home of Leslie Knope.
Fictional towns and cities.Smallville: Smallville is Superman's Kansas hometown, which was the Smallville series' title.
Fictional towns and cities.Whoville: Whoville is the town of Whos in Dr. Seuss's How the Grinch Stole Christmas!
Fictional towns and cities.Stars Hollow: Stars Hollow is the Connecticut town in Gilmore Girls, known for town meetings and quirky festivals.
Fictional towns and cities.Hogsmeade: Hogsmeade is the wizarding village near Hogwarts, the only all-magical settlement in Britain, and home to Honeydukes.
Fictional towns and cities.Kalamazoo: Kalamazoo is a real city in Michigan, with a famous song, 'I've Got a Gal in Kalamazoo'.
Fictional towns and cities.Timbuktu: Timbuktu is a real city in Mali, and was a medieval center of learning.
Fictional towns and cities.Walla Walla: Walla Walla is a real city in Washington state, famous for sweet onions and its name, said to mean 'many waters'.
Fictional towns and cities.Ouagadougou: Ouagadougou is a real city, the capital of Burkina Faso, with a name that is fun to say.
Fictional towns and cities.Punxsutawney: Punxsutawney is a real Pennsylvania town, where groundhog Phil predicts the weather each February.
Fictional towns and cities.Ypsilanti: Ypsilanti is a real Michigan city, named for a Greek independence leader.
Fictional towns and cities.Schenectady: Schenectady is a real New York city, historically GE's home, with a name from a Mohawk word.
Fictional towns and cities.Tuscaloosa: Tuscaloosa is a real Alabama city, home of the University of Alabama and named for a Choctaw chief.
Fictional towns and cities.Chattanooga: Chattanooga is a real Tennessee city, in a 1941 song, 'Chattanooga Choo Choo'.
Fictional towns and cities.Tallahassee: Tallahassee is Florida's real capital, a name from a Muskogean word for old town.

Herding dog breeds.Border Collie: Widely seen as the smartest breed, it herds sheep with an intense stare called 'the eye', no barking or biting needed.
Herding dog breeds.Australian Shepherd: Despite the name, the breed took shape in the American West; Basque shepherds arriving via Australia gave it its label.
Herding dog breeds.German Shepherd: Captain Max von Stephanitz bred it in 1890s Germany as the ideal working herder; it later became the classic police dog.
Herding dog breeds.Corgi: These short-legged herders nipped cattle's heels and ducked the kicks; Queen Elizabeth II owned over thirty in her life.
Herding dog breeds.Old English Sheepdog: Its shaggy coat was once sheared for spinning, and the old docked tail earned it the nickname 'bobtail'.
Herding dog breeds.Shetland Sheepdog: A miniature collie-like herder from Scotland's Shetland Islands, bred small to suit the tiny local ponies and sheep.
Herding dog breeds.Belgian Malinois: Named for the Belgian city of Malines, it is now a favorite of police and military units for its drive and speed.
Herding dog breeds.Briard: A French sheepdog with a long shaggy coat and double dewclaws on its hind legs, said to have guarded flocks since the Middle Ages.
Herding dog breeds.Kelpie: Australia's tireless sheepdog is said to run across the backs of packed sheep to reach the front of a flock.
Herding dog breeds.Bearded Collie: A bouncy Scottish drover's dog whose long coat parts naturally down the middle of its back.
Herding dog breeds.Puli: This Hungarian herder's corded coat looks like dreadlocks and shields it from weather and predators.
Herding dog breeds.Rough Collie: Made famous by Lassie, who was always played by male dogs, since males keep a fuller coat year-round.
Herding dog breeds.Beagle: A scent hound bred to track hares, so it follows its nose rather than a shepherd's whistle.
Herding dog breeds.Poodle: Originally a water retriever, not a herder; the fancy show clip began as a way to help swimmers move while protecting joints.
Herding dog breeds.Bulldog: Bred for bull-baiting, a sport banned in England in 1835, not for herding; today it is a famously mellow companion.
Herding dog breeds.Dachshund: Its German name means 'badger dog': bred to dive into burrows after prey, not to round up flocks.
Herding dog breeds.Greyhound: A sighthound that chases by speed, not by herding; it can sprint at about 40 mph.
Herding dog breeds.Pug: Bred as a lapdog for Chinese emperors, it has plenty of charm and no herding instinct whatsoever.
Herding dog breeds.Great Dane: Despite the name, this giant boar-hunting breed comes from Germany, not Denmark, and is no herder.
Herding dog breeds.Chihuahua: The smallest dog breed, named for a Mexican state, is purely a companion, not a herder.
Herding dog breeds.Labrador: A retriever from Newfoundland (not Labrador) bred to haul fishing nets, with webbed toes that make it a strong swimmer.
Herding dog breeds.Boxer: Developed in Germany from mastiff-type hunting dogs, it was a guard and cattle-holding dog, not a true herder.
Herding dog breeds.Dalmatian: Famous as carriage dogs that ran beside horse-drawn coaches, they are born pure white and grow their spots later.
Herding dog breeds.Shih Tzu: Its name means 'lion dog'; bred as a Chinese palace companion, it was never asked to herd anything.
